AFRI0090.name: An Introduction to Africana Studies
AFRI0090.description: This course introduces students to the vibrant and contested field of Africana Studies by critically exploring and analyzing the links and disjunctures in the cultural, political, and intellectual practices and experiences of people of African descent throughout the African diaspora. Beginning with a critical overview of the history, theoretical orientations, and multiple methodological strategies of the discipline, the course is divided into three thematic units that examine intellectuals, politics, and movements; identity construction and formation; and literary, cultural, and aesthetic theories and practices in the African diaspora.

AFRI0390.name: African(a) Media and the Gender-Diversity Question?
AFRI0390.description: This course explores African and Africana media, including literature, film, digital storytelling, visual culture, and social media as dynamic sites where gender diversity, sexuality, race, class, kinship, citizenship, and economic power are imagined, negotiated, and transformed. This course challenges colonial epistemologies, Western ethnographic narratives, and heteronormative assumptions of gender and sexuality that have long shaped representations of African(a) societies. Students will examine the continent and its diasporas from an intersectional lens through shared historical and social processes that produce and regulate gendered, sexed, and sexual subjects across time and space. By analyzing creative works alongside critical scholarship, students will develop a nuanced understanding of how African and Africana cultural productions contest colonial systems of gender classification and exclusion while generating new possibilities for gender and sexual diversity, cultural belonging, and social justice in an increasingly global and interconnected world.

AFRI0553.name: The World Has AIDS
AFRI0553.description: This course explores the cultural production of the HIV/AIDS pandemic from across Africa, contemplating not only how such texts grapple with the virus and making life in the face of devastation, but also how they imagine a global habitat. Memoirs of the pandemic, including Levin’s Aidsafari, will inform our exploration of individual self-fashioning and relationality in a world of AIDS. Fiction and media representations of the pandemic, including Kgebetli Moele’s The Book of the Dead and video footage of the 1985 Live Aid concerts, will motivate important discussions about race, the nation-state, surveillance, and global development. Throughout the course, we will also explore how academic work imagined and reimagines the HIV/AIDS pandemic in Africa and beyond, turning to Neville Hoad’s recent book Pandemic Genres and Douglas Crimp’s famed 1987 essay, “How to Have Promiscuity in an Epidemic.”

AFRI1111.name: Systemic Racism and Modes of Resilience
AFRI1111.description: Over the past several years there has been much public discussion about systemic racism, and its role in perpetuating racial inequality. What is systemic racism? What role does it play in society and how have African Americans responded to it? This course will use the lens of “systemic racism” to explore the interconnections between policies and practices that create a network of devastating forms of racial discrimination and disadvantage; conditions that have shifted over time and have made it difficult for black communities, and individuals within them, to flourish. And yet, systemic racism does not have the final word. We will also consider how African-American communities have developed various modes of resilience in cultural, spiritual/religious, artistic, and other facets of life.

AFRI1112.name: What's Popping: The Contemporary Black Theatre Workshop
AFRI1112.description: Open to all Brown students, this course introduces students to contemporary (post-1980) Black theatre history, theory, and artistic practice. Students will read, analyze and interpret a range of influential plays such as What to Send Up When It Goes Down, Hurt Village, Twilight, Topdog/Underdog, Choir Boy, Bootycandy, Diary of a Mad Black Woman, and Fences. Course work includes opportunities to perform scenes and monologues, see live theatre in and around Providence, and devise original performance works through in-class writing, movement, and improv theatre exercises. The semester culminates in an Artists Salon featuring students' work. No previous acting, improv, movement, directing, playwriting or Black theatre experience required. No prereqs. All are welcome.

AFRI1161.name: The Truth Will Set you Free
AFRI1161.description: This course sets out to understand how nations reimagine themselves and how individuals fashion lives in the aftermath of mass violence and mass death—what it means to inhabit this global era of reconciliation. Among other questions, we will consider: What is reconciliation? What does successful reconciliation look like? Is truth-telling always a means to reconciliation? Are reconciliation and forgiveness one and the same? Focusing specifically on the African continent, we will examine collective trauma and political reconciliation in part through the framework of the state- and NGO-sponsored truth commission. Our initial study of South Africa’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission will provide an entry point into our later study of Zimbabwe’s Gukurahundi Genocide and Rwanda’s Gacaca courts. We will move beyond these commissions to consider how cultural production functions in response to or as part of a reconciliatory project.

AFRI1232.name: Listening Closely to Bob Marley and the Wailers: Race, Religion and Radicalism in the Seventies
AFRI1232.description: How can we locate Bob Marley and the Wailers in the global Black political upheaval of the late 60s and early 70s? How can we understand the influences that helped to forge Marley’s perspectives, from Garveyism, to Rastafarianism, Black Power and other local radical trends? How in turn did Marley and the Wailers music impact upon and help to influence popular movements, from anti-War movements in the United States, to anti-nuclear movements in Europe, anti colonial struggles in Africa and Oceania, postcolonial resistance against neocolonialism in the Caribbean, and above all, the anti-Apartheid resistance in South Africa? How might we understand Marley’s Rastafarian ideology and what were its peculiarities as an ideology of human liberation? And more than four decades after Marley's death, what, if anything, remains of his message in a post-postcolonial time?

AFRI1330.name: Africana Studies Junior Seminar
AFRI1330.description: This junior seminar course is designed to support students’ growth as academic writers and will prepare them to better complete their culminating senior thesis projects. While specifically geared towards Africana Studies concentrators, the class is open to any undergraduate student who has successfully completed AFRI 0090: An Introduction to Africana Studies and at least four semesters of coursework overall towards the Bachelor’s degree. Course materials will delve deeply into the history, spaces, peoples and cultures of the African Diaspora, exploring a selection of critical writings, performance pieces, fiction and non-fiction works by leading scholars and artists.

AFRI1400.name: Fashion, Gender, and Identity Politics in African(a) Media
AFRI1400.description: This course examines fashion, the practices of dress, adornment, and bodily presentation, as a critical lens for understanding the social, political, economic, and cultural histories of Africa from the late nineteenth century to the present. Grounded in African and Africana Studies, the course treats fashion as a form of material culture and historical evidence through which Africans have expressed identity, exercised agency, negotiated power, and responded to changing local and global conditions. A central question guides the course: How have changing fashions across Africa reflected and shaped the concerns, aspirations, and anxieties of women, men, youth, and marginalized communities over time? Students will engage with a wide range of sources, including scholarly texts, novels, comic strips, graphic novels, newspapers, films, documentaries, podcasts, digital and street art, museum collections, fashion photography, and social media.

AFRI2003.name: Performing Blackness: Critical Acts
AFRI2003.description: This course approaches the study of race and performance through the fields of Africana Studies and Performance Studies to investigate how and why human beings endow bodies with social meaning. It resists biological determinist narratives about race, and instead approaches the study of Blackness as embodied cultural practice transmitted from generation to generation. Course materials will encourage students to consider why “blackness” persists as an organizing force in human societies, and how Black performance as an object, method, and/or analytic reveals how people make, break, and transform the world.

AMST0192W.name: Faultlines: Race, Art, and the American Landscape
AMST0192W.description: What does it mean to change “landscape” from a noun to a verb? This seminar explores how American environments have been constructed, contested, and reimagined. From the frontier of the American West to outer space (the “final frontier”), we will treat both extraordinary and everyday landscapes as living archives. We will examine plantations, national parks, trash heaps, and sites like the San Francisco Bay, the Sonoran Desert, and Providence for their layered histories. Drawing from environmental history, cultural studies, and critical race and ethnic studies, we will ask: how does art help us read contested landscapes? We will engage with photography, film, creative nonfiction, performance, and painting, with workshops at the Nature Lab, RISD Museum, and sessions with local artists. No prerequisites or art background needed––we will observe, experiment, and make things together. WRIT course, limited to first-years and sophomores.

AMST0192X.name: Sex in the Digital Age
AMST0192X.description: This seminar examines sex and sexuality in the digital age, turning to the Internet, as well as other sites of digitally-mediated encounters, to better understand contemporary formations of intimacies. We will traverse digital sites, online communities, literature, popular culture media, and art to investigate dating and hookup apps, queer community formations, cruising, porn, OnlyFans, robots, AI, and speculative fiction, amongst others. Tracing both the lineages and trajectories of sex in the digital age, topics of conversation will range from feminist debates about the ethics of pornography in the 70s and 80s to the increasing prevalence of AI companionship and anxieties around technological futures. Our course will use critical scholarship, considering race, gender, and sexuality to interrogate politics of belonging, desirability, and intimacy in our increasingly digitized world. Limited to first-years and sophomores, no prerequisites.

AMST0601J.name: Popular Culture in the United States
AMST0601J.description: This course is part of the American Studies “Questions” series, fulfilling an introductory-level requirement for the AMST concentration. The course surveys the relationship between society and culture and will introduce you to major themes in the field that have emerged in recent years. The core mission of the class is to connect popular culture to the larger world in which it is produced and consumed. We explore how culture is used to establish and contest social boundaries in the contemporary United States and examine how diverse cultural fields such as popular music, film, and social media both reflect and drive social change. Registration priority for first-years and sophomores, others may request overrides if space available. No prerequisites.

AMST1900T.name: Disability: History, Theory, and Bodily Difference
AMST1900T.description: This seminar explores the history of disability across cultural, legal, medical, and political dimensions of American life.  We will consider the changing meanings of disability, the history of disability activism and communities, representations of disabilities, and the relationship between technology and the body. We will also discuss the intersections between disability and other categories of difference such as gender, race, and sexuality.

AMST1907C.name: James Baldwin (ENGL 1711S)
AMST1907C.description: Interested students must register for ENGL 1711S.

AMST1907L.name: Forming Latinx Literature
AMST1907L.description: Forming Latinx Literature is an advanced seminar in reading contemporary Latinx fiction. The class is designed to introduce you to an array of Latinx writers and to hone your attention to both the form and craft of fiction. The class will introduce you to critical readings from the school of neo-formalism as well as essays about the craft of writing and interpreting fiction. Goals of the course include introducing you to a relevant critical vocabulary for discussing form, deepening your reading abilities, and improving your oral and written communication skills.

AMST1907M.name: Nationalizing Narratives: Race, Nationalism, and the American Novel (ENGL 1710M)
AMST1907M.description: Interested students must register for ENGL 1710M.

AMST1907N.name: Harlem Renaissance: The Politics of Culture (ENGL 1710I)

AMST1907P.name: Music and Disability (MUSC 1246)

AMST1907R.name: Films that Teach: Education, Advertising, Propaganda, and Persuasion in Modern America
AMST1907R.description: We live in a world shaped by screens that teach, persuade, and influence how we think, work, consume, and participate in public life. That world has a history. Rather than focusing on Hollywood films and commercial television, this course explores a vast archive of the twentieth century’s “useful” nonfiction audiovisual media: educational films, industrial and corporate promotion, advertising, public health initiatives, propaganda, and more. Examining these overlooked media as historical evidence, students will investigate how social experts, businesses, and the state have used audiovisual communications to shape everyday life. We consider how these films speak to American cultural and political life and how their techniques continue to inform contemporary message-driven media environments.

AMST2221L.name: Native Feminist Thought
AMST2221L.description: This graduate seminar explores Native Feminisms as a theoretical framework that destabilizes settler colonialism’s gendered and racialized projects of dispossession. Students will trace a genealogy of Native Feminisms, exploring questions of gender variance, roles, and (interspecies) relationalities within Native and Indigenous communities. We will ask how these have been challenged and adapted under settler colonialism. This course also asks how Native Feminists differentiate and press at the limits of what has been termed “Whitestream Feminism” while also asking how Native Feminisms demand intersectional engagement with Black, Latinx, and Transnational Feminisms. In this class, we will ask: What are the anti- and decolonial possibilities of Native Feminist organizing? How do Native Feminists address gendered violence as a symptom and tool of settler colonial dispossession? And, what is the role of intersectional relationality and eroticism in cultivating otherwise worlds and temporalities?

AMST2221N.name: Popular Science (HMAN 2402M)

AMST2520.name: American Studies: Professional Issues in American Studies
AMST2520.description: This course explores the mechanics of a doctorate degree in American Studies. We will explore the constitution of our field through the elaboration of field exam lists and narratives, query its pedagogical application in the design of undergraduate syllabi, and begin to outline and enact our participation in the profession both within and beyond the academy. At the end of this class, students will have constructed a portfolio that will assist their progress towards a degree and provide the tools with which to chart pathways once a degree is in hand. S/NC

AMST2660.name: Projects in Public Humanities
AMST2660.description: Devoted to one or more advanced projects in Public Humanities not covered in detail by the regular courses. Projects in public humanities provide practical, hands-on project and group project management experience that is essential for careers in museums, historic preservation, and cultural agencies. Students will work with faculty advisor to project completion. Written permission and topic description required. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course. This course is repeatable for credit. ANTH0100.name: Introduction to Cultural Anthropology
ANTH0100.description: This course is an introduction to cultural anthropology, the study of human society and culture. Cultural anthropology "makes the strange familiar, and the familiar strange," challenging ingrained assumptions about the human condition, popular understandings of human societies, and conventional wisdom on cultural difference. Anthropologists primarily work toward these ends through ethnography, the long-term, intensive study of different social groups. Students will learn to conduct and analyze ethnographic research as a way of understanding society and cultural difference. This course will introduce some of the major topics in cultural anthropology including culture, race, gender, sexuality, colonialism, class, the state, medicine, and modernity.

ANTH0112.name: Anthropology for Global Leaders
ANTH0112.description: This course makes the case that global leaders have much to gain from anthropology, the study of human diversity across geographic and historical contexts. Readings and lectures will introduce students to anthropological thinking about significant global challenges - namely climate change, the internet, and international migration. We will discuss appropriate methods of translating academic knowledge into policy and action. The course will also use anthropological literature to explore what constitutes effective and ethical leadership in a global context. Assignments will encourage students to develop and practice their own leadership skills, including skills of analysis, communication, and group organization.

ANTH0350.name: Suffering and Compassion
ANTH0350.description: One might say that to be human is to suffer, but what is suffering? Is it to be avoided or embraced? To what ends? The answers to these questions are not just personal or psychological. Rather, they are deeply sociocultural and historical. Orientations toward suffering shape major aspects of life, such as religion, politics, humanitarianism, and medicine. This course explores different ways that society and culture create suffering, and ways that suffering shapes society and culture. This happens not just in suffering itself but also in ways that people try to overcome suffering. Therefore, we also consider the relationship of compassion, empathy and sympathy, and other forms of care to suffering, always paying close attention to questions of the unequal distributions of both suffering and compassion to different groups of people.

ANTH0500.name: Past Forward: Discovering Anthropological Archaeology
ANTH0500.description: This course offers a broad journey through the human past, from material culture crafted by our evolutionary ancestors to the remnants of the recent historic past.  To facilitate this journey, the class explores the methods, concepts, and theories that anthropologists employ in the study of past peoples, places, and things. Case studies stretch across the globe.  As a hands-on endeavor, archaeology focuses on tangible evidence.  In this course, small-group discussion, laboratory, and field exercises will complement lectures, leading to an understanding of how anthropologists study the past and how that knowledge affects the present.

ANTH0775.name: Farm to Table: Foodways and Gastro-Politics in the Ancient Near East (ARCH 0775)
ANTH0775.description: Interested students must register for ARCH 0775.

ANTH1202.name: Oceanic Methods, Archipelagic Thinking, and Tidal Ethnographies (HMAN 1201A)
ANTH1202.description: Interested students must register for HMAN 1201A.

ANTH1215.name: The Anthropology of Aging
ANTH1215.description:
In a recent article entitled “Aging is the Real Population Bomb”, Bloom and Zucker describe a world that is being disrupted by the changing shape of the population pyramid. By 2050, it is estimated that one in six people worldwide will be over 65, up from just one in eleven in 2019. This shift is reshaping everything—from healthcare demands and pension systems to labor markets and technological innovation.
In this course we will examine the experiences of growing old. We will explore what it means to grow old within societies, families, workplaces, and social networks. We will examine prevalent attitudes and stereotypes about age and aging that shape interpersonal and institutional practices.  Through an examination of lived experiences, cultural beliefs, and social practices, we will develop a clear understanding of the experience of aging.

ANTH1242.name: Bioethics and Culture
ANTH1242.description: This course examines bioethics from an ethnographic point of view. Topics include pregnancy, death, suicide, disability, medical research, organ transplantation, and population control. We will distinguish between the moral experiences of people faced with difficult choices, and the ethical ideals to which they aspire. We will then ask: how can these perspectives be reconciled? When trying to reconcile these perspectives, how can we account for powerful dynamics of race, gender, class, religion, and cultural difference? Finally, how can we develop a code of ethics that takes these issues into account and also is fundamentally connected to everyday life?

ANTH1329.name: Anthropology of Things: Culture and Circulation of Commodities
ANTH1329.description: We will examine familiar things from unfamiliar angles—and across time—where we will learn how commodities connect people and places historically, and why those connections continue to matter in the present. You will produce a field-based analysis of a commodity of your choice, gaining practical experience in ethnographic observation, data interpretation, and critical analysis of how commodities circulate, acquire value, and shape everyday life.

ANTH1510A.name: Theorizing Reproductive In/Justice
ANTH1510A.description: Reproductive Justice, a theoretical paradigm and activist praxis developed by Black feminist organizers in the U.S., provides a framework for analyzing how reproduction is shaped by power structures. In this course, students will learn to examine pressing contemporary issues related to reproduction through the lens of anthropology. By examining the RJ movement’s primary three principles, 1) the right not to have a child, 2) the right to have a child, and 3) the right to parent children in safe and healthy environments, this course welcomes junior scholars into an interdisciplinary space for thinking through the historical and continued role of governance strategies in shaping and controlling reproduction, and reproduction’s impact and reliance on seemingly disparate aspects of life.

ANTH1558.name: Queer Ethnography
ANTH1558.description: Is there such a thing as a queer ethnographic sensibility? This class will explore queer ethnography in its many iterations, paying close attention to how anthropologists and other theorists have understood and brought together two notoriously slippery terms—queer and ethnography. We will examine texts formally designated as queer ethnography alongside multidisciplinary media exploring queer life in order to determine if queer ethnography involves, or even demands, a particular approach or sensibility. Readings will introduce students to topics in medical anthropology, Black studies, anthropology of empire, diaspora studies, visual anthropology, and the use of ethnographic writing outside of anthropology. Through these readings, screenings, and listening exercises, students will develop an understanding of the varied and occasionally contentious criteria for what makes some anthropology, and ethnography, “queer.”

ANTH1622.name: Archaeology of Settler Colonialism
ANTH1622.description:
The course uses settler colonialism as a framework for understanding how European colonists attempted to displace and eliminate Indigenous peoples beginning in the 15th century and its historical implications for structural inequalities of race and gender. We will look at how settler colonialism is different from colonialism, and more importantly, at resistances challenging its ambitions. Case studies from North America mostly, but also Australia, South Africa, and other settler colonial societies will focus on historical
archaeology’s contributions to illuminating settler colonialist strategies for establishing and maintaining settler sovereignty in light of concerns for decolonizing archaeological practices. We will give special attention to the insights gained about the experiences of dispossessed, enslaved, and marginalized peoples and their descendants, and the many ways their actions critiqued settler colonialism and imagined different futures.

ANTH1654.name: Queer Times: Present, Future, Past (GNSS 1554)
ANTH1654.description: Interested students must register for GNSS 1554.

ANTH1760.name: The Body and the World: Disability and Culture in Everyday Life
ANTH1760.description: Like gender and race, disability is a cultural and social formation that identifies particular bodies and minds as different, regularly as undesirable, and rarely as extraordinary. This course introduces the theoretical, cultural, and political models of disability and explores the lived experiences of persons with disabilities across time and within different social contexts. Through a discussion of scholarly readings, literature, film, photography, art, and archaeology, this seminar considers disability in relation to: identity; impairment; stigma; monstrosity; marginalization; discrimination; beauty; power; media representations; activism; intersectionality; and gender and sexuality.

ANTH1773.name: Bioarchaeology and Forensic Anthropology (ANTH 1775)
ANTH1773.description: Interested students must register for ARCH 1773.

ANTH1775.name: Animals in Archaeology (ARCH 1775)
ANTH1775.description: Interested students must register for ARCH 1775.

ANTH1930.name: Anthropology Thesis Workshop
ANTH1930.description: This course is a year long two-semester workshop (offered in the fall and spring semesters) for students who are researching and writing an honors or senior thesis in Anthropology or a closely related field. Supplementing advisor support, the course will introduce students to best practices, shoring up essential skills in research design, methods, data interpretation, and written and oral presentation. Students will also participate in peer review, offering and responding to substantive and supportive feedback on their work in progress. The workshop, which meets every other week, is structured so that students can make substantial progress, following a recommended schedule to ensure the successful and timely completion of the thesis in the spring.

ANTH1940.name: Ethnographic Research Methods
ANTH1940.description: To understand the different theoretical assumptions that shape research efforts; to examine how hypotheses and research questions are formulated; and to appreciate the ethical and scientific dimensions of research by hands-on experience in fieldwork projects. Prerequisite: One Anthropology course.

ANTH1970.name: Individual Research Project

ANTH2001.name: Race, Sex, Capital (GNSS 2001)
ANTH2001.description: Interested students must register for GNSS 2001.

ANTH2045.name: Proposal Writing Workshop for Anthropological Fieldwork
ANTH2045.description: This course is designed for third-year graduate students in any subfield of anthropology or closely related fields who are writing grant proposals for dissertation research. Student grant proposals will be pre-circulated and workshopped. Students will gain familiarity with the format for writing successful proposals, with the strategies needed to operationalize them, and with the everyday academic labor of both offering and responding to substantive feedback.

ANTH2060.name: Anthropology Dissertators' Seminar
ANTH2060.description: This seminar is for post-field graduate students in residence at Brown who are at any stage of writing their dissertations. It is intended to support dissertators by providing a structured community, providing a setting for sharing goals, and workshopping writing.

ANTH2150.name: Writing Ethnography
ANTH2150.description: What is ethnography? What makes an anthropological text a vivid and compelling ethnography? How is ethnography different from (and similar to) other forms of producing knowledge about human experience, such as journalism or narrative nonfiction? How do ethnographers establish authority through writing? How do ethnographers engage with questions of ethics and politics of witnessing and storytelling? This graduate seminar is part critical examination of ethnography as a genre of knowledge production and representation and part writing workshop focused on the craft of ethnographic writing. Throughout the semester students will 1) read ethnographies and discuss their features; 2) read about the craft of writing and explore strategies and techniques for portraying characters and describing places and events; and 3) practice writing ethnographically through short in-class exercises and longer written assignments.

ANTH2202.name: Advanced GIS and Spatial Analysis
ANTH2202.description: This course develops students’ skills in geographic information systems and spatial analysis beyond those taught in Anthropology 1201 or other introductory GIS courses, with the goal of facilitating advanced, independent research. The course begins with a rapid review of data models, spatial data management, and thematic mapping, which is designed to quickly bring students with less formal GIS training up to speed. We then move on suitability modeling, network analysis, intermediate spatial statistics, and scripting, with a focus on developing competencies across multiple software platforms, including QGIS, ArcGIS Pro and R. Some topics can be further adjusted to meet student needs and interests. There are no formal prerequisites but an introductory course in GIS (such as Anthropology 1201) is highly recommended.

ANTH2253.name: Transnational Feminist Politics and Knowledge Production
ANTH2253.description: This interdisciplinary graduate seminar aims to de-center and decolonize discussions about feminism(s) by focusing on transnational feminist politics and knowledge production. Course readings and discussions will engage theoretical and methodological tools associated with transnational feminist politics and decolonizing knowledge. At the same time, the course will provide concrete empirical examples of struggles, strategies and forms of feminist resistances emanating from the Middle East, Latin America, Africa and South Asia.  The course will encourage students to ask questions about transnational feminist solidarities and knowledge productions as well as power imbalances, tensions and conflicts within and between feminist groups and initiatives.

ANTH2970.description: For graduate students who have met the tuition requirement and are paying the registration fee to continue active enrollment while preparing for a preliminary examination.

APMA0160.name: Introduction to Scientific Computing
APMA0160.description: For students in any discipline that may involve numerical computations. Includes instruction for programming in MATLAB. Applications discussed include solution of linear equations (with vectors and matrices) and nonlinear equations (by bisection, iteration, and Newton's method), interpolation, and curve-fitting, difference equations, iterated maps, numerical differentiation and integration, and differential equations. Prerequisites: MATH 0100 or equivalent.

APMA0200.name: Introduction to Modeling
APMA0200.description: This course provides an introduction to the mathematical modeling of selected biological, chemical, engineering, and physical processes, and the use of computational tools that facilitate the modeling. The goal is to illustrate the typical way in which applied mathematicians approach practical applications: understanding the underlying problem, creating a model, analyzing the model using mathematical techniques, and interpreting the findings in terms of the original problem. Single-variable calculus is the only requirement; techniques from differential equations, linear algebra, numerical methods, probability, statistics, and MATLAB programming will be introduced in class. Prerequisites: MATH 0100 or equivalent.

APMA0260.name: Linear Algebra and Multivariable Calculus for Applied Mathematicians
APMA0260.description: This one-semester course provides an integrated introduction to multi-variable calculus and linear algebra. Students will develop a strong foundation in mathematical concepts and techniques essential for the applied mathematics concentration. Prerequisites: MATH 0100 or equivalent.

APMA0350.name: Applied Ordinary Differential Equations
APMA0350.description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to ordinary differential equations and their applications. During the course, we will see how applied mathematicians use ordinary differential equations to solve practical applications, from understanding the underlying problem, creating a differential-equations model, solving it using analytical, numerical, or qualitative methods, and interpreting the findings in terms of the original problem. This course is geared towards methods for solving ordinary differential equations rather than the underlying theoretical foundations. Prerequisites: MATH 0100 or equivalent; knowledge of matrix-vector operations, determinants, and linear systems. Linear algebra is strongly recommended as a prerequisite or corequisite.

APMA0355.name: Applied Ordinary Differential Equations with Theory
APMA0355.description: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to ordinary differential equations, their applications, and their theoretical underpinnings. During the course, we will see how applied mathematicians use ordinary differential equations to solve practical applications, from understanding the underlying problem, creating a differential-equations model, solving it using analytical, numerical, or qualitative methods, and interpreting the findings in terms of the original problem. We will also learn about the underlying rigorous theoretical foundations of differential equations and the mathematical formalism used to establish this theory. Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; Linear algebra.

APMA0360.name: Applied Partial Differential Equations I
APMA0360.description: This course provides an introduction to partial differential equations and their applications, with an emphasis on techniques for solving PDEs rather than theory. We will learn how to use partial differential equations to solve problems that arise in practical applications by formulating questions about a real-world problem, creating a partial differential equation model that can help answer these questions, solving the resulting system using analytical, numerical, and qualitative methods, and interpreting the results in terms of the original application. Topics include the four fundamental PDEs (transport, wave, heat, and Laplace equations), solution techniques (Fourier transform, energy methods, separation of variables, maximum principles), and example applications. Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; APMA 0350 or equivalent.

APMA0365.name: Applied Partial Differential Equations I with Theory
APMA0365.description: This course provides a rigorous introduction to partial differential equations and their applications. Emphasis will be placed on the theoretical foundations of partial differential equations and the mathematical formalism used to establish this theory. We will learn how to use partial differential equations to solve problems that arise in practical applications by formulating questions about a real-world problem, creating a partial differential equation model that can help answer these questions, solving the resulting system using analytical, numerical, and qualitative methods, and interpreting the results in terms of the original application. Topics include the four fundamental PDEs (transport, wave, heat, and Laplace equations), solution techniques (Fourier transform, energy methods, separation of variables, maximum principles), and example applications. Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; Linear algebra; APMA 0355 or equivalent.

APMA0650.name: Introduction to Probability and Statistics
APMA0650.description: A first course in probability and statistics without calculus. Topics include data fluency, probability spaces, discrete and continuous random variables, expected values, law of large numbers, central limit theorem, point estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, measures of association, linear regression. Examples and applications from the popular press and the life, social and physical sciences.

APMA1080.name: Inference in Genomics and Molecular Biology
APMA1080.description: This course is an introduction to the probabilistic and statistical models that have found widespread use in genomics and molecular biology. The emphasis is on foundational models and ideas rather than practical application. Likely topics include Markov chains, hidden Markov models, directed graphical models, mixture models, linear regression, regularization, dimensionality reduction, clustering, Bayesian inference, and multiple hypothesis testing. Examples will focus on the connection to genomics and molecular biology, but all of these tools have found widespread use in a variety of disciplines. Mathematical and computational exercises will reinforce the topics presented in lecture. Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; Linear algebra; Computer programming; APMA 1655 or equivalent.

APMA1170.name: Introduction to Computational Linear Algebra
APMA1170.description: Focuses on fundamental algorithms in computational linear algebra with relevance to all science concentrators. Basic linear algebra and matrix decompositions (Cholesky, LU, QR, etc.), round-off errors and numerical analysis of errors and convergence. Iterative methods and conjugate gradient techniques. Computation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and an introduction to least squares methods. Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; Linear algebra. Experience with a programming language is strongly recommended.

APMA1210.name: Operations Research: Deterministic Models
APMA1210.description: An introduction to the basic mathematical ideas and computational methods of optimizing allocation of effort or resources, with or without constraints. Topics include linear programming, network models, dynamic programming, and integer programming. Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; Linear algebra; Computer programming.

APMA1330.name: Applied Partial Differential Equations II
APMA1330.description: Review of vector calculus and curvilinear coordinates. Partial differential equations. Heat conduction and diffusion equations, the wave equation, Laplace and Poisson equations. Separation of variables, special functions, Fourier series and power series solution of differential equations. Sturm-Liouville problem and eigenfunction expansions. Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; Linear algebra; APMA 0365 or equivalent.

APMA1650.name: Introduction to Probability and Statistics with Calculus
APMA1650.description: A first course in calculus-based probability and statistics. Topics include data fluency, probability spaces, discrete and continuous random variables, expected values, law of large numbers, central limit theorem, point estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, measures of association, linear regression. Examples and applications from the popular press and the life, social and physical sciences. Prerequisites: MATH 0100 or equivalent.

APMA1655.name: Introduction to Probability and Statistics with Theory
APMA1655.description: A first course in calculus-based probability and statistics. Topics include data fluency, probability spaces, discrete and continuous random variables, expected values, law of large numbers, central limit theorem, point estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, measures of association, linear regression, and example applications. This course introduces students to the mathematical theory and formalism needed for upper-level undergraduate courses in probability and statistics. Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; Linear algebra.

APMA1690.name: Computational Probability and Statistics
APMA1690.description: Examination of probability theory and mathematical statistics from the perspective of computing. Topics selected from random number generation, Monte Carlo methods, limit theorems, stochastic dependence, Bayesian networks, dimensionality reduction. Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; Linear algebra; APMA 1655 or equivalent; Programming experience is recommended.

APMA1860.name: Graphs and Networks
APMA1860.description: Selected topics about the mathematics of graphs and networks with an emphasis on random graph models and the dynamics of processes operating on these graphs. Topics include: empirical properties of biological, social, and technological networks (small-world effects, scale-free properties, transitivity, community structure); mathematical and statistical models of random graphs and their properties (Bernoulli random graphs, preferential attachment models, stochastic block models, phase transitions); dynamical processes on graphs and networks (percolation, cascades, epidemics, queuing, synchronization). Prerequisites: Multivariable calculus; Linear algebra; APMA 0355 or equivalent; APMA 1655 or equivalent; programming experience. APMA 1200 or APMA 1690 or similar courses recommended.

APMA1931B.name: Mathematical Foundations of Machine Learning
APMA1931B.description: This course provides a proof-driven introduction to the mathematical foundations of machine learning, emphasizing when and why learning is possible. The course develops learning-theoretic tools—empirical risk minimization, PAC generalization guarantees, VC dimension, and uniform convergence—and connects them to canonical models and algorithms such as linear regression, kernel methods, and neural networks as well as optimization methods including stochastic gradient descent. Students synthesize the theory through a final project: reading a research paper on theoretical machine learning or closely related area, and delivering a paired presentation, alongside an individual written report.

APMA1931C.name: Applied Complex Analysis
APMA1931C.description: This course provides an exploration of the magical world of complex numbers, with focus on applications. Topics covered include: Basics of Complex Numbers, Analytic Functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations, Cauchy's Integral formula, Residue Theorem, Evaluation of Integrals. Familiarity with reading and writing proofs will be assumed, but no analysis or linear algebra background is required. Prerequisites: Multivariable Calculus, Partial Differential Equations.

APMA1970.name: Independent Study
APMA1970.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

APMA1971.name: Independent Study -  WRIT
APMA1971.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course. This course should be taken in place of APMA 1970 if it is to be used to satisfy the WRIT requirement.

APMA2110.name: Real Analysis
APMA2110.description: Provides the basis of real analysis which is fundamental to many of the other courses in the program: metric spaces, measure theory, and the theory of integration and differentiation.

APMA2190.name: Nonlinear Dynamical Systems I
APMA2190.description: Basic theory of ordinary differential equations, flows, and maps. Two-dimensional systems. Linear systems. Hamiltonian and integrable systems. Lyapunov functions and stability. Invariant manifolds, including stable, unstable, and center manifolds. Bifurcation theory and normal forms. Nonlinear oscillations and the method of averaging. Chaotic motion, including horseshoe maps and the Melnikov method. Applications in the physical and biological sciences.

APMA2550.name: Numerical Solution of Partial Differential Equations I
APMA2550.description: Finite difference methods for solving time-dependent initial value problems of partial differential equations. Fundamental concepts of consistency, accuracy, stability and convergence of finite difference methods will be covered. Associated well-posedness theory for linear time-dependent PDEs will also be covered. Some knowledge of computer programming expected.

APMA2570B.name: Numerical Solution of Partial Differential Equations III
APMA2570B.description: We will cover finite element methods for ordinary differential equations and for elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic partial differential equations. Algorithm development, analysis, and computer implementation issues will be addressed. In particular, we will discuss in depth the discontinuous Galerkin finite element method. Prerequisite: APMA 2550 or equivalent knowledge in numerical methods.

APMA2630.name: Theory of Probability I
APMA2630.description: Part one of a two semester course that provides an introduction to probability theory based on measure theory. The first semester (APMA 2630) covers the following topics:  countable state Markov chains, review of real analysis and metric spaces, probability spaces, random variables and measurable functions, Borel-Cantelli lemmas, weak and strong laws of large numbers, conditional expectation and beginning of discrete time martingale theory.  Prerequisites—undergraduate probability and analysis, co-requisite—graduate real analysis.

APMA2670.name: Mathematical Statistics I
APMA2670.description: The course covers advanced modern methods for high dimensional parametric statistical learning theory. Topics include: (1) Maximum likelihood and Bayesian parameter and set estimation for both iid data and Graphical Models; (2) Linear regression including ridge regression, lasso, principal components, and study of issues such as model selection and overparametrization; (3) Linear classification including Bayesian classification, discriminant analysis, Fisher discriminant analysis, flexible discriminant analysis, support vector machines, and perceptron; (4) Classical and Bayesian hypothesis testing; (5) Coherent presentation of Markov Graphical Models, Hidden Graphical models, and computational algorithms for optimization and simulation such as Markov Chain Monte, Dynamic Programming, and Bootstrap; (6) Infinite data asymptotics for inference and phase transitions for Markov Graphical Models. Prerequisite: APMA 2630 or equivalent.

APMA2812K.name: Probabilistic Dynamics on Large Graphs
APMA2812K.description:
This advanced topics course studies probabilistic models of large graphs and stochastic processes evolving on them, following Rick Durrett’s Dynamics on Graphs. The course develops rigorous tools from probability theory to analyze random graph models, interacting particle systems, and network-based stochastic dynamics.
Topics include Erdős–Rényi and related random graph models, branching process and exploration techniques, phase transitions, and scaling limits, as well as dynamic processes on graphs such as epidemic models, contact processes, and voter-type systems. Emphasis is placed on asymptotic analysis, coupling arguments, and mean-field and high-dimensional methods that are central to current research in probability.
The course is intended for advanced graduate students with a strong background in measure-theoretic probability and stochastic processes.

APMA2980.name: Research in Applied Mathematics
APMA2980.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

APMA2990.name: Thesis Preparation
APMA2990.description: For graduate students who have met the residency requirement and are continuing research on a full time basis.

APMAXLIST.name: Courses of Interest to Students Majoring in Applied Mathematics

ARAB0100.name: First-Year Arabic
ARAB0100.description: Builds basic listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills, introducing the Arabic language in its cultural environment. Four contact hours per week, with an emphasis on grammar and communication, plus written, audio, and video assignments outside of class. This is the first half of a two-semester sequence course whose first semester grade is normally a temporary one. Neither semester may be elected independently without special written permission. The final grade at the end of the course work in ARAB 0200 covers the entire year and is recorded as the final grade for both semesters. If course is full, please request an override.  Enrollment limited to 18.

ARAB0300.name: Second-Year Arabic
ARAB0300.description: Develops listening, speaking, reading and writing skills at the intermediate level of language proficiency through extensive use of various texts and multimedia. Promotes better understanding of Arabic cultural traditions. Five contact hours weekly, plus written, audio, and video assignments outside of class. Prerequisite: ARAB 0200. This is the first half of a year-long course. Neither semester may be elected independently without special written permission. The final grade at the end of the course work in ARAB 0400 covers the entire year and is recorded as the final grade for both semesters.

ARAB0500.name: Third-Year Arabic
ARAB0500.description: This course offers comprehensive training in listening, speaking, reading, and writing at the advanced proficiency level. It will accelerate students’ advancement toward language and cultural proficiency by integrating the study of Modern Standard Arabic and Colloquial Arabic, the latter of which will be the main form of oral communication in class discussions. Thematic units will include selections from the classical and modern traditions of Arabic writing, contemporary film and media, and various art forms with the goal of broadening students’ understanding of Arab societies and their cultures. Through this integrated approach, students will gain confidence to function in an ample variety of social and cultural environments and access a wider range of media. Prereq: ARAB0400 or equivalent

ARAB0700.name: Advanced Arabic:  Tales of the City
ARAB0700.description: The Arab city, current site of a major political upheaval, is the central theme of this integrated-skill language and culture course. Images of cities, as multifaceted as the people who inhabit them, animate cinema screens and daily news reports, inspire masters of writing, artists, and musicians, arouse political activism. By engaging the complex representation of the urban theme in contemporary discursive and art forms, this course will enhance students' understanding of the dynamics of urban politics and culture in the Middle East, while building a content-specific lexicon and advanced communicative ability. Prerequisite: ARAB 0600, or an equivalent. Enrollment limited to 12.

ARAB1990.name: Special Topics in Arabic Language, Literature, and Culture
ARAB1990.description: Advanced level integrated skill course focusing on specific reading and writing topics derived from the traditions and arts of the Arabic language. Course prerequisites include advanced capacity in Arabic grammar and reading comprehension. Enrollment limited to 10.

ARCH0100.name: Field Archaeology in the Ancient World
ARCH0100.description: Always wanted to be Indiana Jones? This course, focusing on the Mediterranean world and its neighbors in antiquity, interprets field archaeology in its broadest sense. In addition to exploring "how to do" archaeology - the techniques of locating, retrieving, and analyzing ancient remains - we will consider how the nature of these methodologies affects our understanding of the past.

ARCH0172.name: South Asian Art and Architecture (HIAA 0023)
ARCH0172.description: Interested students must register for HIAA 0023.

ARCH0295.name: Crafts and Production in the Ancient World: Making Material Culture
ARCH0295.description: The manufacture of artifacts distinguishes us from all other species. However, archaeologists often struggle with interpreting material culture without understanding its origins and production. This course will examine how things are made, considering craftsmanship and agricultural production, from raw materials to finished objects: sculpture and mosaics, bricks and concrete, ceramic and glass, metallurgy, tanneries, oil, wine, and perfumes. Through case studies and hands-on activities, students will consider the importance of the technological processes that produce artifacts for archaeology’s investigation of our human past.

ARCH0396.name: Sacred Spaces: Synagogues, Churches, Mosques (JUDS 0050P).
ARCH0396.description: Interested students must register for JUDS 0050P.

ARCH0524.name: Art and Architecture of the Roman Empire (HIAA 0032)
ARCH0524.description: Interested students must register for HIAA 0032.

ARCH0775.name: Farm to Table: Foodways and Gastro-Politics in the Ancient World
ARCH0775.description: This course provides an introduction to the culture, economy, and politics of food in the ancient world. We will not only investigate the day-to-day of food production, consumption, and disposal; we will also develop an appreciation for changing food fashions, for the etiquette of eating and drinking, and for the complex world of gastro-politics. Through case studies, we will explore topics such as subsistence and diet, feasting, food security, power, race and ethnicity, and gender. We will even explore the ancient kitchen using our own hands, mouths, and stomachs as a guide.

ARCH1051.name: Archaeology of Settler Colonialism (ARCH 1622)
ARCH1051.description: Interested students must register for ANTH 1622.

ARCH1128.name: The Long Fall of the Roman Empire (HIST 1205)
ARCH1128.description: Interested students must register for HIST 1205.

ARCH1208.name: Globalism before Globalization: The Interconnected World of the Early Middle Ages (HIST 1954F)
ARCH1208.description: Interested students must register for HIST 1954F.

ARCH1272.name: Troy:Fact, Fiction, Impact (CLAS 1240)
ARCH1272.description: Interested students must register for CLAS 1240.

ARCH1273.name: Xenophon’s Anabasis: Empire, Contact, Archaeology (CLAS 1520)
ARCH1273.description: Interested students must register for CLAS 1520.

ARCH1544.name: Heritage in the Metropolis: Remembering and Preserving the Urban Past (URBN 1871A)
ARCH1544.description: Interested students must register for URBN 1871A.

ARCH1626.name: Gods, Mummies, and Myths: Exploring Ancient Egyptian Society (EGYT 1050).
ARCH1626.description: Interested students must register for EGYT 1050.

ARCH1634.name: The Crossroads of Three Continents: Ancient Egypt’s History from the Collapse to Cleopatra EGYT 1435
ARCH1634.description: Interested students must register for EGYT 1435.

ARCH1773.name: Bioarchaeology and Forensic Anthropology
ARCH1773.description: Bioarchaeology and forensic anthropology have common methodological roots (human osteology) but are oriented to answer very different questions. Both are grounded in the anthropological sub-disciplines of biological anthropology and archaeology. The focus in bioarchaeology is advancing our understanding of the human experience in the past. Bioarchaeologists study a range of topics including health, violence, migration, and embodiment. Forensic anthropology is a form of applied anthropology that is employed to document and interpret human remains in medico-legal contexts. The course will survey both fields while instructing in the methodologies and approaches of each. The course complements The Human Skeleton (ARCH 1772/ANTH 1720).

ARCH1775.name: Animals in Archaeology
ARCH1775.description: Food, foe, friend: animals play all these roles, and more, in their relationship to humans, in the past as well as the present. This course will explore how zooarchaeology -- the study of animal remains (bones, teeth, and shells) -- allows us to reconstruct ancient human-animal-environmental interactions. We will cover a range of topics and analytical techniques, including hands-on sessions for the identification and quantification of faunal remains. Additional topics will include ancient DNA in zooarchaeology, bone stable isotope analyses, human-caused extinctions, animal domestication, bone artifact production, and animal sacrifice. Enrollment limited to 20. Not open to first year students.

ARCH1845.name: The Archaeology of Textiles
ARCH1845.description: Humans need the warmth – and social capital – clothes provide, ships need cloth to sail, sheep and flax need pastures and fields. Fabric and its production have shaped our physical and cultural environments for millennia. But cloth’s ephemeral nature makes it nearly invisible in the archaeological record – and biases against so-called women’s work have rendered fabric production similarly unseen in scholarship. Through hands-on learning, students in this class will process fiber, spin with a spindle, and weave on a loom we build. Students will connect this practice with their own research, investigating the production and use of ancient textiles in student-driven case studies.

ARCH1872.name: Environmental Anthropology (ANTH 1555)
ARCH1872.description: Interested students must register for ANTH 1555.

ARCH1886.name: Introduction to Spatial Digital Humanities (HMAN 1300B)
ARCH1886.description: Interested students must register for HMAN 1300B.

ARCH1891.name: Alien Writing: Invented Scripts from Demons to Dune (ASYR 1020)
ARCH1891.description: Interested students must register for ASYR 1020.

ARCH1900.name: The Archaeology of College Hill
ARCH1900.description: A hands-on training class in archaeological field and laboratory techniques. Topics include the nature of field archaeology, excavation and survey methodologies, archaeological ethics, computer technologies (such as GIS), and site and artifact analysis and conservation. Students will act as practicing archaeologists (i.e., actually dig and analyze the results!) through the investigation of local historical and archaeological sites in the College Hill area (e.g. the First Baptist Church of America and Brown University's Quiet Green).

ARCH1970.name: Individual Study Project in Old World Archaeology and Art
ARCH1970.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

ARCH1990.name: Senior Honors Thesis in Archaeology and the Ancient World
ARCH1990.description: Honors students in Archaeology and the Ancient World who are completing their theses should enroll in this course in their final semester. The subject of the thesis and program of study will be determined by the needs of the individual student. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

ARCH2112.name: Roman Epigraphy (LATN 2120A)
ARCH2112.description: Interested students must register for LATN 2120A.

ARCH2153.name: Archaeological Ethnography: A Multi-Temporal Contact Zone
ARCH2153.description: In this course, we will critically examine the emerging, hybrid field of archaeological ethnography, a shared space of interaction between social anthropologists and archaeologists, and between scholars and the various local communities around archaeological sites. What does it mean for archaeologists to engage with ethnography? How can materiality and temporality provide the focus for creating the transcultural, shared space of archaeological ethnography? How can this emerging field transform the disciplines of archaeology and anthropology?

ARCH2157.name: Subaltern Communities: Archaeological Perspectives Beyond Domination and Resistance
ARCH2157.description: Mediterranean (pre)history is usually cast in terms of an inexorable rise of state domination and colonial exploitation under the euphemistic label of ‘social complexity’. This seminar will examine and highlight the role of ‘people without history’ not by simply pitching them as rebels against dominant powers but by exploring the subtle and manifold connections that interweave subaltern communities with hegemonic groups.

ARCH2858.name: Advanced GIS and Spatial Analysis (ANTH 2202)
ARCH2858.description: Interested students must register for ANTH 2202.

ARCH2950.name: Intensive Readings in Ancient Language for Archaeologists
ARCH2950.description: In this course, students with some previous training in an ancient language will have an opportunity to hone their linguistic skills while reading ancient texts that are specially relevant to archaeologists. The primary purpose of the course is to prepare students to take doctoral ancient language exams and to identify weak spots in individuals' knowledge of the ancient language. Emphasis will be placed on identification and justification of morphology and syntax, as well as on reading comprehension and idiomatic translation.

ARCH2970.name: Preliminary Examination Preparation
ARCH2970.description: Reading, research, and preparation of one of the three Preliminary Exam Essays required for doctoral students in Archaeology and the Ancient World. Students are expected to enroll in this course three times, each with the appropriate instructor by topic. Can be taken three times for credit. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check course listings for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

ARCH2976.description: Reading, research, and preparation for, and completion of, one of the two Field Exams in a secondary field of study for doctoral students in Archaeology and the Ancient World. Students are expected to enroll in two sections of this course, each with the appropriate instructor by topic. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check course listings for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

ARTS1018.name: People Falling Together and Apart:  Writing Romantic Screenplays
ARTS1018.description: People Falling Together and Apart: Writing Romantic Screenplays is an in-person workshop with weekly assignments intended to build a foundation in narrative screenwriting for a romantic film. The course covers idea development, story breakdown, screenplay form and revision. Each practical step is paired with discourse on romance as a film genre. There will be consistent critique of work, which includes peer evaluation. The expected outcome is a production ready romantic short screenplay.

ARTS1019.name: Art CAMP: Critical Art Methods + Practice
ARTS1019.description: Art CAMP launches first-year students into the robust arts ecosystem at Brown University, inviting them to experience the arts as an essential part of campus life and intellectual inquiry. Each week, students will attend an arts program of their choosing then develop creative responses in any medium, encouraging students to build a sustainable arts practice on campus. Class discussions will be grounded in critical readings, providing a framework for arts research and practice. By the end of the course, students will have mapped pathways for engaging with the arts across campus, developed strategies for sustaining a creative practice, and learned how to access arts resources to support their academic research. The course positions the arts not as separate from academic life, but as a vital, generative force that can deepen inquiry and support meaningful engagement across fields of study.

ARTS1020.name: Breaking Baumol: The Economics of Nonprofit Arts
ARTS1020.description: Breaking Baumol introduces students to the predominant business models employed by US-based arts and cultural organizations, and the contradictions and conflicts those businesses bring to bear. For years nonprofit organizations have proliferated throughout the arts. While these “charitable” organizations are granted benefits to both increase revenue and decrease expenses, they have resulted in an arts sector that is overly-reliant on old ways of working with systemic inequities regarding power and control, allergic to change, and continuously struggling with the same operating concerns and risks. Using the Brown Arts Institute and other local organizations as case studies, students will interrogate the business model by examining when it works, where it doesn’t work, and why it has persisted over time. The course is a primer for undergraduate and graduate students interested in creative careers and/or concentrations from the arts departments.

ARTS1550.name: Robots (re)Imagined: Art, Engineering, and Speculative Futures
ARTS1550.description: Robots (re)Imagined is a first-of-its-kind collaboration between RISD, the Brown Arts Institute, and Brown Engineering, bringing artists, designers, computer scientists, and engineers together to develop new vocabularies for robotics and art. Robots have long mirrored our collective hopes and anxieties. But what if they could do something else entirely: something poetic, unpredictable, transformative? This course operates as both studio and experimental research lab. Students design and program robots that move beyond utility, building machines that sense, act, and communicate in ways that unsettle boundaries between the technical and the aesthetic. The semester culminates in a public presentation, hosted by BAI, of interdisciplinary projects expanding the social, ethical, and imaginative possibilities of twenty-first-century robotics.

ARTS1970.name: Brown Arts Institute Independent Study
ARTS1970.description: ARTS Independent study offerings create opportunities for students throughout the University to work with Brown Arts Institute faculty to develop courses designed to explore art-related topics of interest with a tailored and focused approach. Once the department and BAI faculty advisor approve, students may register for an independent study or research project. Any student wishing to pursue an independent study or research project must submit a proposal by the first day of the shopping period for the semester in which the proposed project will be conducted. Submit your proposal via this form for official registration approval: https://forms.gle/x7xeiwWdg2f7zBWSA

ASYR0510.name: The Zodiac: A 3000 Year History of Horoscopes, Astronomy, and Imagination
ASYR0510.description: "What's your star sign?" Just about everyone has been asked this question at one time or another. But what is a "star sign"? Astronomically, it's the sign of the zodiac in which the sun was located at your birth. Astrologically, it can mean anything from you'll have a long life to don't take out a loan. In this course we will explore the history of the concept of the zodiac and its use in astronomy and astrology from its invention by ancient Babylonian astronomers up to today. We'll find out why the Roman emperor Augustus adopted the symbol of the zodiacal sign Capricorn, why the zodiac is depicted on the floors of ancient synagogues, how Kepler used the zodiac when interpreting the star of Bethlehem, and how astronomers ancient and modern use it when calculating positions of the planets.

ASYR0800.name: The Cradle of Civilization? An Introduction to the Ancient Near East
ASYR0800.description: This course explores the cultures of ancient Mesopotamia and the Near East (present-day Iraq, Syria, Turkey, and Iran) from prehistory until the end of the first millennium BC. We will investigate the rich history and archaeology of this region through literary and historical texts (in translation) and archaeological evidence, including visual culture and architecture. Central to our discussion will be questions about how and why scholars study the Middle East in this early period. Topics include: early complex societies, state formation, the origins and development of writing, ancient empires, religion, culture and ethnicity, trade, diplomacy, warfare, agriculture, and craft production.

ASYR1020.name: Alien Writing: Invented Scripts from Demons to Dune
ASYR1020.description: This class is an exploration of human graphic ingenuity, and also of human limitations in the attempt to imagine how human and non-human others write (and read). We will examine ancient magical treatises, fantasy literature, Hollywood blockbusters and B-movies, and video-games to ask: Why do people invent writing systems for fictive worlds? What can writing systems used by devils and demons or angels and aliens tell us about writing systems invented and used by humans (such as Mesopotamian cuneiform, Egyptian hieroglyphs, Viking runes, and the Cherokee syllabary)? How are “con-scripts”—writing systems invented for fictive worlds—different from and/or similar to other writing systems? Why do people learn to write in Tolkien’s cirth or to “read” magical charakteres?

ASYR1990.name: Individual Study Project
ASYR1990.description: Directed reading and research arranged with individual faculty. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

ASYR2310A.name: Ancient Scientific Texts: Akkadian
ASYR2310A.description: Readings and analysis of a major scientific text in Akkadian. Prerequisite: AWAS 0200 or 0210. Open to graduate students only.
