ENGN2912E.description: Integrated circuits drive today’s technologies, from smartphones and wearable devices to AI systems and supercomputers. Building on the fundamentals developed in ENGN 1600 and related courses, this project-based course takes students through the complete journey from a chip idea to a verified design. Through lectures, hands-on labs, and a team project, students gain advanced experience with Verilog, simulation, synthesis, physical design, and verification. Students will be introduced to agentic frameworks and learn to use AI as an engineering partner for design, verification, and debugging while critically evaluating AI-generated results. By the end of the semester, students will be prepared to tackle advanced digital and system-on-chip designs using skills increasingly valued in research and the semiconductor industry. An optional tapeout in GlobalFoundries 180 nm technology allows students to bring their designs to silicon.

ENGN2912H.name: Interfacial Phenomena
ENGN2912H.description: This course is an introduction to mechanics of material interfaces. Particular cases considered are liquid surfaces (surface tension, contact line slip, electro-wetting, etc), lipid membranes, and thin elastic plates and shells. The course will cover detailed analyses of statics and dynamics of these interface. Classical and modern research papers related to these topics will form the motivation for the discussion. A unified treatment of these apparently disparate interfaces is presented to conclude the course. Prerequisites: ENGN 2010, 2020, 2210, or 2810.

ENGN2912T.name: Experimental Fluid Mechanics
ENGN2912T.description: Theory and practice of experimental techniques for fluid mechanics. Principles of measurement, noise and error analysis, transduction and recording of signals. Measurement of temperature and pressure. Fundamentals of optics and image processing for measurements, Particle Image Velocimetry and Particle Tracking Velocimetry. Microfluidic and wind tunnel experimental techniques. Will include lab projects.

ENGN2960.name: Experiential Learning in Industry (ELI)
ENGN2960.description: This course will immerse students for up to 6 months in a corporate environment to learn first-hand about industry careers in engineering and technology. Corporate environments may include design, development, simulation, testing, technical documentation, consulting, investment, patent law, licensing, compliance, and/or regulations. Students will work as employees for a host company and carry out company-defined activities.

ENGN2970.name: Preliminary Examination Preparation
ENGN2970.description: For graduate students who have met the tuition requirement and are paying the registration fee to continue active enrollment while preparing for a preliminary examination.

ENGN2980.name: Special Projects, Reading, Research and Design
ENGN2980.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

ENGN2990.name: Thesis Preparation
ENGN2990.description: For graduate students who have met the residency requirement and are continuing research on a full time basis.

ENVS0070H.name: The Plants and Animals of College Hill
ENVS0070H.description: This course explores the natural history of organisms living in our own urban environment with a mix of lecture, readings, classroom study of organisms, and close to weekly outside explorations of College Hill, where we will identify species, study their behavior and explore the ecological basis for their survival. The course will explore how these urban-dwelling species provide benefits for our own health and wellbeing, some of the inequities that people have in access to biodiverse green spaces within urban areas, and the role that cities can play in species conservation. Students will gain basic species-identification and observation skills, utilize and add to existing online, citizen-science databases that record species occurrences, and conduct a small term project that explores the diversity or behavior of a specific taxonomic group or organism at a study site of their choosing on College Hill.

ENVS0110.name: Humans, Nature, and the Environment: Addressing Environmental Change in the 21st Century
ENVS0110.description: This is an engaged scholars course that offers an introduction to contemporary environmental issues. We explore the relationships between human societies and the non-human environment through a survey of topical cases, including: human population growth and consumption, global climate change, toxins, waste streams, water resources, environmental justice and ethics, and agro-food systems. This course also analyzes various solutions—social, political, technical, and economic—put forth by institutions and individuals to address questions of environmental sustainability. Each student must register for a 50-minute weekly engaged scholar lab in addition to lectures. Each lab will partner with a community organization to complete an engaged, environmental project.  See class notes for reserved seating registration set up by semester level.

ENVS0192W.name: Faultlines: Race, Art, and the American Landscape (AMST 0192W)
ENVS0192W.description: Interested students must register for AMST 0192W.

ENVS0465.name: Climate Solutions - A multidisciplinary perspective
ENVS0465.description: This course will explore solutions to the climate crises through the lens of multiple disciplines.  Lectures will cover topics in physical science, economics, political science, persuasive communication, social science, and equity.  Online lectures by disciplinary experts from around the country, but developed specifically for this class, will be the basis for the in class discussions and activities led by Brown Faculty.

ENVS0717.name: Ocean Conservation: Ecology, Management, and Politics
ENVS0717.description: This course examines ocean conservation, focusing on design, implementation, and effects on ecosystems and people. The use of marine protected areas and marine spatial planning has rapidly increased, and interest in alternative energy, food security, and marine biodiversity conservation has heightened both the use and critique of these tools. Using interdisciplinary team learning, guest visits by practitioners, and traditional lectures, we will explore questions such as: What can spatial management tools do (and not do)? How are they created and managed in particular contexts? Who gets to decide and why? We will explore cases in Rhode Island, Hawai'i, Bermuda, and the high seas to understand ecological and social factors that can lead to management success or failure. Students will write a management plan proposal for a coastal area, including ecological justification, social aspects and implications, and a long-term implementation plan.

ENVS0732.name: Environmental Impact Assessment: Opportunities and Challenges
ENVS0732.description: This course introduces environmental impact assessment (EIA) in the United States as a legal, technical, and political process for evaluating proposed development and environmental change. We will examine the major stages of impact assessment, including screening, scoping, alternatives analysis, significance, public participation, mitigation, and follow-up. Students will learn how EIA operates in practice through close attention to federal and state procedures, environmental assessment documents, and controversies surrounding infrastructure, energy, coastal development, waste, and environmental risk. This course is for everyone and will be particularly rich with participation from students with a range of interests spanning biology, engineering, policy and government, energy transitions, Indigenous politics, STS, sociology (and more). This course is framed to situate EIA within broader debates about expertise, democracy, environmental justice, and Indigenous sovereignty. We will draw primarily from Federal and Rhode Island-based case studies.

ENVS0733.name: Introduction to Environmental Law and Policy
ENVS0733.description: This course introduces students with no legal training to the core institutions, statutes, and debates that shape U.S. environmental law and policy. Rather than providing a framework to ‘think like lawyers,’ this course encourages students to read, question, and use environmental law as engaged citizens, professionals, and policy advocates. The course centers on both federal and Rhode Island law and policy while drawing on case studies to situate abstract concepts into practical approaches to environmental care. Students will be asked to think critically about rules and decision-making through an environmental justice lens: who/what does environmental law protect, and who does it burden? Case studies threaded throughout the semester examine environmental law and policy through the lenses of race, class, gender, labour, and Indigeneity. Tribal sovereignty and U.S. Tribal environmental law run as a throughline across the term.

ENVS0830.name: Water in Our World (EEPS 0830)
ENVS0830.description: Interested students must register for EEPS 0830.

ENVS1207.name: Eco-Entrepreneurship
ENVS1207.description: Environmental, business, and social opportunities are often seen as being at odds. This course is a hands-on, interactive journey to explore bringing an impactful idea for an environmental product/service/solution into the world and designing a business plan to do so. You will identify an environmental area of opportunity, learn how to focus on the problem before the solution, identify the key stakeholders including your users/customers, and build a business model. You will look at the triple bottom line, and learn new tools, best practices, and frameworks to breathe life into your solution and make it viable. Instructions for submitting a personal statement before enrolling will be available in the syllabus.

ENVS1247.name: Clearing the Air: Environmental Studies of Pollution
ENVS1247.description: Whether air, water or land borne, pollution is a multivalent “wicked problem” that has profound implications for the climate, ecological and economic systems, and human health and well-being. Emphasizing engaged scholarship based in Providence, we will explore pollution’s historical origins, review current pollution measurements and reduction/mitigation efforts, and discuss alternative approaches that better address pollution’s historical legacies and resulting social and environmental inequalities. Coursework will revolve around a Providence-based air monitoring project, augmented by readings, guest lectures, and discussion. Assessment will involve participation in discussion, 2-3 response papers and a final project linked to an engaged, field-study.

ENVS1400.name: Sustainable Design in the Built Environment
ENVS1400.description: Course develops students’ analytical abilities to apply fundamental concepts of environmental issues, building systems analysis, and architectural and engineering design. Students learn how to reduce the negative environmental impacts, and maximize positive social and economic impacts, of the built environment. Students cultivate applied skills in sustainable design; including fundamental energy calculations, heat flow analysis, schematic design analysis, and building operating impacts assessment. Course emphasis is on building energy flows. Students conduct group and independent research projects, providing the opportunity to study broader impacts of the built environment and propose solutions. Class meetings combine lectures, student presentations, and group workshops.  To join the waitlist if there are no available seats, please enter an override request reason and briefly summarize your learning objectives in Courses@Brown. Your concentration and semester information is automatically entered.

ENVS1415.name: Power, Justice, and Climate Change
ENVS1415.description: Climate change is a crisis of power and justice whose consequences are distributed unevenly along lines of class, ethnicity, gender, and race. Those who have contributed the least to the problem often suffer its most severe impacts. These inequalities contribute to the “compounded vulnerabilities” many communities experience and have frustrated efforts to reach ambitious agreements in United Nations climate negotiations. The course examines the social, political, and ethical dimensions of climate change across local, national, and global scales, including adaptation efforts, media narratives, climate denialism, and the rise of climate-justice movements. Enrollment is limited to 40.

ENVS1544.name: Climate and Nature Innovation Lab: From Ideas to Impact
ENVS1544.description: The decisions we make today will determine the future of the planet for generations to come. In this hands-on, interdisciplinary course, students will explore the intersection of climate action, sustainability, finance, and innovation. Through collaborative projects, real-world case studies, guest lectures from environmental leaders, and mentorship, students will confront the realities of environmental degradation, reflect on its personal and collective impact, and identify root causes of pressing environmental challenges. Students will then design scalable, impact-driven solutions, focusing on real-world implementation. Emphasis is placed on creative problem-solving, systems thinking, and sustainable business modeling. Many of the most impactful innovations happen at the intersection of diverse fields and lived experiences. This course welcomes students of all academic disciplines and encourages a broad mix of perspectives, backgrounds, and skills.

ENVS1545.name: The Theory and Practice of Sustainable Investing
ENVS1545.description: 21st century businesses and investors face a broadening and deepening array of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) risks and opportunities. Climate change, water scarcity, community conflicts, resource depletion, supply chain breakdowns, worker well-being and economic inequality pose present material challenges that make sustainability an imperative for successful corporations and investors. We will examine current ESG strategy, trends, future scenarios, players, and frameworks and integrate that theory with practical investment performance analysis, metrics, and study of screens, asset classes, and diversification.

ENVS1558.name: Global Environmental Justice: Dams, Data, War, and More
ENVS1558.description: This is a course about the politics and practices of environmental justice organizing around the world. Using a comparative case study approach, we explore place-based, socio-environmental conflicts involving dams, data centers, wars, tourism, energy transitions, waste, and more in a variety of global locations. Throughout our study, we ask: Who struggles for environmental justice (EJ) and under what conditions? When and why are EJ mobilizations successful? How do repertoires of contention differ by political and ecological context, and by the type of conflict? What is common among spatially and sectorally divergent EJ struggles? And is there a global EJ movement? Course materials draw from critical and decolonial perspectives and scholarship, with a final project that offers students the opportunity to collaborate with the Environmental Justice Atlas.

ENVS1574.name: Climate Policy Research: Organizations and Obstruction
ENVS1574.description: Over three decades, sufficient and equitable policies addressing the crisis of climate change have been elusive, and US leadership is crucial for an adequate global response. After several weeks of readings and lectures on climate policy, the course shifts to team-based research to produce strategic, policy-relevant briefings and scholarly outputs, some with partner organizations. Students will travel to D.C. for five days in October to attend meetings with experts and staff from government agencies, industry organizations, think tanks, journalists and environmental NGOs, and to hold briefings on our joint research.

ENVS1580.name: Environmental Stewardship and Resilience in Urban Systems
ENVS1580.description: This course investigates current environmental impacts and risks related to urban infrastructure systems. Students analyze efforts to minimize negative environmental, health and economic impacts of the built environment. The course explores urban initiatives to increase sustainability and resiliency of infrastructure systems in anticipation of increased risks related to climate change. The goal is to learn the rationale, process and technical aspects of the practice of environmental stewardship and resilience planning in an urban context. Students will develop competence in technical analysis, policy analysis, and program implementation through case studies and systems analyses.

ENVS1615.name: Climate Change, Human Rights, and the Policy Process
ENVS1615.description: The diminishing quality of Earth’s systems and resources carries profound implications for the fulfillment of human rights and aspirations. But even as Western knowledge systems understand better the intrinsic interdependencies between humans and the non-human, policy gridlock persists. Indeed, scientific findings are regularly contested on political grounds. The purpose of this course is to learn how to apply diverse knowledges from Indigenous to Modern to map the relevant policy in problems at the intersection of human rights and environmental integrity, and to develop approaches to address them in ways that are creative, effective, responsible and just.

ENVS1825.name: Commodity Natures: Supply Chains From Extraction to Waste and Alternatives to Endless Growth
ENVS1825.description: What goes into the things we use everyday? Who makes commodities and under what conditions? What happens to stuff after we throw it away? Are we stuck with mass consumption? Are there workable alternatives? These are the kinds of questions we will unpack. Reading from commodity and discard studies, and political economy and ecology, we will situate economic growth in social and environmental context. We will look at production, extraction, circulation, disposal, and afterlives of commodities, with particular attention to invisibilized labor and environmental externalities. And we will explore sustainability proposals, including circularity, degrowth, and repair. In addition to an individual paper, you will apply analytical tools in a semester-long research project to examine a commodity of your choosing. With peers, you will produce a report, narrative website, video, or web-series to narrate the life and afterlife of your thing.

ENVS1911.name: Narrating the Anthropocene
ENVS1911.description: Narratives are key to how we understand our world—making nonfiction storytelling a critical part of comprehending and acting in a time of environmental crises. Through regular writing practice and discussions of readings and other media—including podcasts and film—this class will examine models for how nonfiction narratives can foster a better understanding of past and present environmental change, imagine an environmentally just future, explain technical information for a broad audience, and support an informed, politically active citizenry. Visits from authors and creators will supplement class discussion, as assignments build toward each student completing an environmentally-focused creative narrative project.

ENVS1915.name: River Histories: Fishes, Floods and the Transformation of Freshwater Ecosystems
ENVS1915.description: As food sources and transportation routes, rivers have long played important roles in human societies, and people have in turn transformed them. Most river histories explore the lives of people living along rivers, but this course will seek to look into the waters and understand how human activity has transformed aquatic ecosystems of rivers and adjoining wetlands. What were the effects of humans constraining rivers within levees, blocking them with dams, and clearing forests from their watersheds to make farmland? The class will also consider transportation, water power, flood mitigation, and conflicts between farmers, fishers, and industrialists over how to use rivers. We will focus on three particularly well-studied rivers, the Mississippi, the Yangtze, and the Rhine (including the Netherlands), though students are encouraged to do research projects of the river of their choice.

ENVS1925.name: Energy Policy and Politics
ENVS1925.description: From coal power to solar power, energy drives economies and increases quality of life world-wide. However, this same energy use can, and often does, lead to severe environmental destruction/pollution and global warming. This course serves as an introduction to energy policy in the United States and also explores global attempts to solve energy problems. This course examines different types of energy sources and uses, different ideological paths driving energy policy, the environmental impacts of energy use, current global and domestic attempts to solve energy problems, and the role of renewable and alternative forms of energy in future energy policy.

ENVS1956F.name: Brazilian Biomes: An Environmental History of Brazil (ENVS 1956F)
ENVS1956F.description: Interested students must register for ENVS 1956F.

ENVS1970.name: Independent Study
ENVS1970.description: First semester of individual analysis of environmental issues, required for all environmental studies concentrators. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.  Instructor override required prior to registration.

ENVS2980.name: Reading and Research
ENVS2980.description: First semester of thesis research during which a thesis proposal is prepared. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course. Instructor override required prior to registration.

ENVS2981.name: Reading and Research
ENVS2981.description: Second semester of thesis research. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course. Instructor override required prior to registration.

EPI0850.name: Fundamentals of Epidemiology
EPI0850.description: What is epidemiology? It is the study of the occurrence and distribution of health-related states and processes in specified populations and the application of this knowledge to control health problems This course will provide learners with a strong foundation in the concepts and methods needed to describe the burden of a disease in communities, identify what causes these poor health outcomes, and evaluate the impacts of interventions meant to improve health.

EPI1700.name: Current Topics in Environmental Health
EPI1700.description: This course is designed to introduce students to the field of environmental health, and demonstrate how environmental health is integrated into various aspects of our lives, both directly and indirectly.  Topics to be covered include: toxic metals, vector-borne disease, food safety, water quality, radiation, pesticides, air quality, hazardous waste, risk assessment, and the role of the community in environmental health.  Several topics will be presented by guest speakers so that students can learn from the expertise of professionals in the field. Enrollment limited to 65.

EPI1720.name: Environmental Exposure Assessments in Practice
EPI1720.description: Exposure assessments are the key to linking environmental contaminants to human health. This course will provide you with a detailed overview of environmental exposure assessment and its role in providing tools and metrics for defining exposures in epidemiological studies. This includes the design of community and personal monitoring studies, the techniques and equipment used for sampling and analysis, and the interpretation of data.  Simultaneously, students will develop and carry out an environmental exposure assessment in the local community and will also learn about and put into practice topics such as community engagement, community surveying, environmental justice, and public health communication strategies.

EPI2120.name: Introduction to Methods in Epidemiologic Research
EPI2120.description: Epidemiology is the systematic study of the distribution, determinants, and deterrents of health in populations, with the goal of reducing negative health outcomes. This terminal introductory course is intended to provide graduate students with a strong foundation in epidemiological research methods and design so they can be critical consumers and users of public health evidence. Students will learn the core principles of research questions, measurement, study design, accuracy, and basic epidemiological measures. This course aims to provide students with the ability to critically appraise health research, emphasizing practical research literacy rather than advanced methodological or statistical training. This course is aimed at MPH and doctoral students who are not specializing in Epidemiology. The course is not open to freshmen or sophomores but may be available for advanced undergraduates with the instructor's permission. There are no formal prerequisites for this course.

EPI2140.name: Principles of Applied Epidemiology
EPI2140.description: Epidemiology quantifies the distribution and determinants of health in populations, with the goal of reducing the burden of negative health outcomes. This intensive introductory course is the first in a methods sequence (followed by PHP 2210 and PHP 2180) and is intended to provide graduate students with a solid foundation in epidemiological concepts in relation to public health. They will use this foundation to build a methodological skill set to enable being critical consumers, users, and producers of research. Students will learn the core principles of research design, bias and confounding, and applied public health and be able to apply their knowledge to critically evaluate and synthesize findings from epidemiological studies and begin producing and communicating their own research products. Collaborative learning is a key component of the course design.

EPI2150.name: Foundations in Modern Epidemiologic Methods
EPI2150.description: The overall objective of this course is to provide students with a strong foundation in epidemiologic research methods. This is the first of a three- or four-course sequence in epidemiological methods aimed at students who expect to eventually conduct their own epidemiological research. The course is designed for students enrolled in a PhD program in the School of Public Health, or who are completing the MPH epidemiology concentration. There will be a strong quantitative focus in this course, and the typical student will also have some introductory knowledge of epidemiology. PHP 2507 or 2510 should be taken concurrently. Undergraduate students, fifth year MPH students, or graduate students not in a public health program may request instructor permission (override) through CAB from the instructor.

EPI2180.name: Interpretation and Application of Epidemiology
EPI2180.description:
Epidemiology is not only the study of patterns of health and disease. It also requires the practice of synthesizing evidence, interpreting findings, and communicating their implications for research, practice, and policy.  Strong conceptual foundations allow epidemiologists to ask meaningful questions, state causal and non-causal frameworks, and interpret findings within complex systems. Practical application translates these concepts into real-world analyses, requiring decisions about data sources, study design, measurement, and analytic strategies. Equally essential is the ability to communicate epidemiologic evidence clearly to diverse audiences, including policymakers, practitioners, and the public. Without clear interpretation and communication, even methodologically rigorous findings cannot inform action.
This course focuses on the interpretation and application of epidemiology through the synthesis of existing evidence, the communication of epidemiologic methods and findings to diverse audiences, and the implementation of selected advanced analytic approaches.

EPI2220B.name: Methods for Nutritional Epidemiology
EPI2220B.description: This course introduces key methods in nutritional epidemiology, focusing on the application of epidemiologic principles and quantitative approaches to study diet and health. Students will learn methods for dietary and body composition assessment, descriptive and causal analyses—including target trial emulation—and the interpretation of common nutritional models. The course also surveys advanced topics such as Mendelian randomization, population-level nutrition research, and emerging areas including omics integration and policy-relevant evidence. Designed for graduate students, visiting fellows, and advanced undergraduates, the course prepares learners to critically evaluate and conduct research on diet and health.

EPI2220F.name: Reproductive, Perinatal  and Early Childhood Epidemiology
EPI2220F.description: This course provides an overview of topics related to reproduction, pregnancy, maternal and child outcomes of pregnancy, and long-term consequences related to reproductive health. Methodological issues unique to reproductive and perinatal epidemiology are discussed, as well as general epidemiologic methods as applied to topics in reproductive and perinatal health. Class sessions will include lectures and discussions of published research studies, with active student participation expected. After several introductory lectures, students will select topics and be responsible for organizing a presentation and discussion under the instructor’s supervision.

EPI2232.name: Modern Foundations of Causal Inference in Epidemiologic Research
EPI2232.description: This course explores the development of causal inference in epidemiology through a close reading of influential methodological papers published between 1976 and 2010. Picking up where Sander Greenland’s 1987 anthology of key epidemiologic methods left off, we trace major innovations that have shaped modern thinking about causality. Our focus is not only on understanding the methods themselves, but also on cultivating the skills needed to engage with complex ideas: reading deeply, presenting clearly, and leading thoughtful discussion. Students will practice distilling challenging material, contextualizing each paper historically and conceptually, and communicating technical content with clarity. Although grounded in epidemiology, the course reflects the interdisciplinary nature of causal inference today, incorporating contributions from biostatistics, econometrics, computer science, and related fields. This is a reading- and discussion-intensive course designed to develop both conceptual fluency and professional communication skills in causal inference.

EPI2250.name: Advanced Quantitative Methods in Epidemiologic Research
EPI2250.description: This course provides students with conceptual and quantitative tools based on counterfactual theory and causal diagrams (e.g., DAGs) to make causal inference using data obtained from observational studies. Causal diagrams will be used to provide alternative definitions of, provide clarifications regarding, or inform minimizing common biases. Non-, semi-, and fully parametric methods for minimizing bias will be discussed. These methods include standard regression, instrumental variables, propensity scores, inverse probability weighting, and marginal structural models. Settings when such methods may not be appropriate will be emphasized. Prerequisite: PHP 2200 and 2511; or PHP 2200 and 2508; or instructor permission.

EPI2490.name: Methods in Pharmacoepidemiology
EPI2490.description: This course will cover applications of epidemiological, biostatistical, and other methods to the study of outcomes of medical interventions (drugs, vaccines, biologics, devices, and procedures) in large numbers of people. The course will focus on more advanced study designs (e.g., sequential target trial emulation) and analytic methods (e.g., high-dimensional propensity score estimation). Methods for evaluating the robustness of study results (i.e., sensitivity and stability analyses) will also be discussed. Formal frameworks of causal inference will be used throughout the course and will be applied to substantive topics in pharmacoepidemiology, vaccine epidemiology, and medical device epidemiology.

ERLY1970.name: Individual Study Project
ERLY1970.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

ERLY1990.name: Thesis Preparation
ERLY1990.description: Required of seniors in the honors program. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

ETHN0090A.name: The Border/La Frontera
ETHN0090A.description: We will examine the historical formation, contemporary reality and popular representation of the U.S.-Mexico border from a bilingual (English-Spanish), multicultural (U.S., Mexican, and Latino), and transnational perspective within the framework of globalization. We will explore the construction of border communities, lives and identities on both sides of the international divide, and pay particular attention to the movement of peoples in both directions. We will read materials, watch films,  and conduct class discussions in English and Spanish.  Comfort and reasonable proficiency in Spanish is required, but native command is not necessary. Enrollment limited to 19 first year students.

ETHN1200K.name: Introduction to Native American and Indigenous Studies
ETHN1200K.description: This class examines and introduces the politics, cultures, histories, representations, and studies of the Native peoples of North America, with a primary focus on the United States, and helps students to develop critical thinking, reading, and writing skills regarding Native American and Indigenous Studies. Although broad in cultural and geographic scope, the course does not attempt to summarize the diverse cultures of the hundreds of Native American tribes across the continent or Indigenous peoples globally. Instead, it focuses on several key issues in the lives of, and scholarship about, American Indian/Native American/First Nations/Indigenous peoples in the US (and beyond).

ETHN1209.name: Contemporary Indigenous Education in North America (NAIS 1209)
ETHN1209.description: Interested students must register for NAIS 1209.

ETHN1751G.name: James Baldwin (ENGL 1711S)
ETHN1751G.description: Interested students must register for ENGL 1711S.

ETHN1751K.name: The Bordering of America: Immigration and US Society
ETHN1751K.description: This course will explore immigration and patterns of immigrant incorporation in the United States. The course begins with a brief history of U.S. immigration and then covers thematic topics such as border enforcement, citizenship, assimilation, and social mobility and their relationship to the immigrant experience. International migration is an inherently political phenomenon. As a result, we will concentrate on the development and implementation of policies designed to control movement across U.S. borders and efforts to regulate who can become a member of the American political community. In this course, our goal is to gain a multifaceted understanding of the sociological underpinnings of international migration and ongoing debates over citizenship and rights in American society.

ETHN1751L.name: Race, War, and Medicine (STS 1700B)
ETHN1751L.description: Interested students must register for STS 1700B.

ETHN1751M.name: Nationalizing Narratives: Race, Nationalism, and the American Novel (ENGL 1710M)
ETHN1751M.description: Interested students must register for ENGL 1710M.

FREN0100.name: Basic French
FREN0100.description: This is the first half of a two-semester course. Four meetings a week for oral practice. One hour of work outside of class is expected every day (grammar/writing, oral practice, reading). Enrollment limited to 15.

FREN0300.name: Intermediate French I
FREN0300.description: A semi-intensive elementary review with emphasis on all four skills (listening, speaking, reading and writing). Class activities include drills, small group activities, and skits. Class materials include videos, a French film, short stories, and various other authentic documents. Prerequisite: FREN 0200 or placement (Previous experience with French is required to take this class). Four meetings per week, plus a 50-minute conversation section with TAs.

FREN0400.name: Intermediate French II
FREN0400.description: Continuation of FREN 0300 but may be taken separately. A four-skill language course that stresses oral interaction in class (three meetings per week plus one 50-minute conversation section). Materials include audio activities, film, and a novel. Short compositions with systematic grammar practice. Prerequisite: FREN 0300, FREN 0200 with permission, or placement.

FREN0500.name: Writing and Speaking French I
FREN0500.description: A four-skill language course that stresses oral interaction in class. Thematic units will focus on songs, poems, a short novel, a graphic novel, films and a longer novel. Activities include a creative project using Comic Life, and a systematic grammar review. Prerequisite: FREN 0400, FREN 0200 with written permission, or placement. Minimum score of 4 in AP French Language

FREN0600.name: Writing and Speaking French II
FREN0600.description: Prerequisite for study in French-speaking countries. Class time is devoted mainly to conversation and discussion practice. Writing instruction and assignments focus on essays, commentaries, and to a lesser degree, on story writing. Apart from reading assignments for discussion (press articles and literary excerpts), students select two novels to read. Prerequisite: FREN 0500 or placement Minimum score of 5 in AP French Language. Enrollment limited to 15.

FREN0720G.name: L'art de la nouvelle
FREN0720G.description: In this course we shall study a range of examples of the nouvelle or short story, from 19th century realist and fantastic literature (Maupassant, Flaubert, Colette) to modern French and Francophone texts (Sartre, Camus, Djebar, Redonnet, Quiriny). Emphasis will be on formal analysis, major genres/movements (realism, the fantastic, existentialism, anti-/post-colonial critique, “post-modernism”) and the short story’s capacity to offer forms of social critique. We will also read some secondary theoretical materials (Freud, Sartre, Barthes, Todorov, Piglia, Samoyault). Taught in French.

FREN0930.name: Africa in Cinema (MCM 0903O)
FREN0930.description: Interested students must register for MCM 0903O.

FREN0970B.name: Sociologies De Paris
FREN0970B.description: This course considers the borders of Parisian urban space: gentrification, de-gentrification, regentrification of neighborhoods, and uneven management of illegal activity. Diverse commemorations of working-class and marginalized memories and histories of Paris will be discussed, including but not limited to the Commune of 1871, the deportations during World War II, and the events of October 17, 1961. Together, we will reflect upon the legacy of French colonization on Parisian urban space (its riches, its different populations) and on the communities of exiles and migrants that lived for a period of time in Paris or settled there in the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries. Particular attention will be paid to the literature, photography and studio arts that inform and inspire sociologists and can serve as documentation or in building knowledge. Taught in French. Course limited to students in Brown-in-France study abroad program.

FREN1040B.name: Pouvoirs de la scène: le théâtre du XVIIe siècle
FREN1040B.description: This course examines how 17th-century theater both reinforces and undermines the ideologies of absolutism, national identity, the nuclear family, and emerging bourgeois consciousness, among others. Special consideration will be given to the theory and performance of theater in the 17th century and the present. Readings will be supplemented with screenings of videos for the plays studied (as available). In addition to papers and oral presentations, students will stage selections from some of the plays studied. Plays by Rotrou, Corneille, Molière, Racine, and an opera by Quinault/Lully. Taught in French. Prerequisite: a course at the 0600 or 0700 level or equivalent proficiency. Contact the instructor to verify your proficiency if you have not taken French at Brown.

FREN1130G.name: Modernismes poétiques
FREN1130G.description: Poetry begins with (more) white space on the page. The modernist remaking of poetry - beginning somewhere in the second half of the 19th century and lasting more or less through the first half of the 20th – brought about an exponential increase in the volume of that space, and in various other extensions of it (e.g. into design and drawing, into the unconscious). The course will briefly examine the origins of those transformations in the 19th century and follow through their ramifications in poets such as Apollinaire, the Surrealists, Cocteau, Bataille and Ponge. Taught in French. Prerequisite: a course at the 0600- or 0700-level or equivalent proficiency. Contact the instructor to verify your proficiency if you have not taken French at Brown.

FREN1330G.name: PENSER À TRAVERS LES YEUX. ÉCRITURE ET PEINTURE
FREN1330G.description: This course will explore how philosophers and writers have viewed painting. The work of the painter, as Gilles Deleuze writes, consists in destroying and standing up to the catastrophe (“the painter must go through a moment when he sees nothing, a collapse of visual coordinates”). We will then reflect upon the challenges that such a catastrophe also poses to the gesture of writing. From Diderot’s Salons to Francis Bacon according to Deleuze, from Velázquez analyzed by Foucault to Vermeer as seen by Proust, we will seek to understand what Jean-François Lyotard calls “thinking through the eyes.” Taught in French. Prerequisite: a course at the 0600- or 0700-level or equivalent proficiency. Contact the instructor to verify your proficiency if you have not taken French at Brown.

FREN1970.name: Individual Independent Study
FREN1970.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course. Instructor permission required.

FREN1990.name: Senior Thesis
FREN1990.description: Independent study in an area of special interest to the student, with close guidance of a member of the staff, and leading to a major paper. Required of candidates for honors, and recommended for all senior concentrators. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

FREN2600Q.name: We Have Never Been Human
FREN2600Q.description: Theories of the limits of human life might begin by analyzing politico-ethical treatments of human beings, or by questioning the bases for distinctions between species. This course will argue that what remains consistently underexamined in such approaches is the human relation to technicity, leaving us ill-equipped to respond to challenges such as AI. By examining the thinking of mostly French philosophers and writers (e.g. Antelme, Blanchot, Bataille, Deleuze, Derrida, Duras, Foucault, Sartre, Simondon, Stiegler) we will attempt to understand first the coming-into-crisis of humanism, and second, different perspectives that emerge as a result of conceiving the human as originarily technological. Course will be conducted in English. FFS students in will read texts in French where appropriate, and write assignments in French.

FREN2980.name: Reading and Research
FREN2980.description: Work with individual students in connection with special readings, problems of research, or preparation of theses. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

FREN2990.name: Thesis Preparation
FREN2990.description: For graduate students who have met the residency requirement and are continuing research on a full time basis.

GISP0003.name: Economics and Aesthetics of the Luxury Industry

GNSS0120.name: Introduction to Gender and Sexuality Studies
GNSS0120.description: Explores the interdisciplinary fields of Gender and Sexuality Studies, considering the relation between formations of gender and those of sexuality across a range of historical and disciplinary contexts. Considers how both sexuality and gender are shaped in relation to race and ethnicity, economic inequality, and the postcolonial legacy.

GNSS1410.name: Gender, Race, and Health
GNSS1410.description: This interdisciplinary seminar addresses how gender, race, and health have been socially and politically constructed and how health inequities across and within racialized and gendered groups have been socially produced over time. We will discuss and apply interdisciplinary theoretical and methodological approaches for critically addressing issues of gender, race, and health, including from critical health studies, gender and sexuality studies, Black studies, and Indigenous studies. Using a case study approach, we will explore key topics pertaining to gender, race, and health, including scientific racism, eugenics, and (bio)medicalization, as well as activism, care, and healing. This course pays particular attention to the lived experiences of Black and Indigenous communities in the Americas, including oppression by and resistance to inequitable social, economic, and political structures, systems, and institutions that shape the social, built, and natural environments in which we live.

GNSS1535.name: American Horror Stories
GNSS1535.description: This course investigates the relationship between institutions and individuals, the general and the personal, and the normal and the monstrous in U.S. horror literature and media. How and why are so many institutions—prisons, hospitals, universities—described in terms of horror, as institutional nightmares? How do horror subgenres—Gothic fiction, body horror, psychological horror, monster stories, zombie narratives—function and what cultural work do they perform? How and to what effect are “monstrous” and “normal” figures racialized and gendered? To address these questions, we will read and view texts in a range of media with emphasis on Asian American and African American literary and cultural production from the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. We’ll explore how horror is not only “about” patriarchal institutions and their fear and management of difference, but also a site of feminist critique and pleasure.

GNSS1541.name: Disturbing the Peace: Black Women in the Arts
GNSS1541.description: How do Black women attain subjectivity through performance and artistic practices? In this course we will explore how writing, visual art, music, and performance by Black women incites conversations, change, joy, and controversy. Black women’s art reveals the hidden and often unspoken conditions of being Black and female, while our creativity often complicates history and reveals uncomfortable truths about artistic fields and institutions. Some artists we will discuss during the course include Ntozake Shange, Betty Davis, Barbara Ann Teer, Elizabeth Catlett, Nina Simone, and Faith Ringold. We will discuss the many risks and the abundant spiritual and intellectual rewards of writing, painting, dancing, sculpting, making music, creating films, and performing while Black and female.

GNSS1554.name: Queer Times: Present, Future, Past
GNSS1554.description: This seminar investigates the queer nature of time—its folds, disjunctures, and loops—taking as a foundational assumption that time is not always a linear phenomenon. In other words, time isn’t always straight. We will take an interdisciplinary approach to studying how time has been reconceptualized in queer theory, physics, trans studies, Black studies, anthropology, and art. What is the relationship between past, present, and future? Do all bodies, people, places, and spaces experience time in the same way? How is time racialized, classed, gendered and sexed in particular ways? What is the relationship between queerness and temporality? And what does it mean to be out of time? We will address these questions through encounters with scholars and artists across spacetime, culminating in a media analysis that explores questions of queer temporality in relation to popular queer films and works of fiction.

GNSS1810.name: Independent Study and Research
GNSS1810.description: Independent reading and research for upper-level students under the direction of a faculty member.  Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

GNSS1962K.name: The Politics of Productivity
GNSS1962K.description: Why are we so obsessed with productivity? This course examines how productivity became the central value of the contemporary work ethic (displacing rival ideals such as craft and vocation) and how the veneration of productivity interacts with gender and race. We begin by exploring classic accounts of labor from philosophy and economics, as well as more recent accounts of technology and automation. The bulk of the course will then focus on how artists and writers have responded to—and often contested—the imperative to be productive. Readings include Karl Marx, the Bible, Adam Smith, Hannah Arendt, Alison Bechdel, George Eliot, Émile Zola, Herman Melville, Toni Morrison, Richard Wright, Caro Claire Burke, Nella Larsen, and Richard Bruce Nugent. Students will write short response papers, analyze a social-media influencer of their choice, and pursue an original research project related to the course’s themes.

GNSS1970.name: Directed Research and Thesis
GNSS1970.description: Independent research under the direction of a faculty member, leading to a thesis. Required of honors candidates. Open to seniors only. Instructor permission required.

GNSS1990.name: Senior Seminar
GNSS1990.description: A research seminar focusing on the research and writing of the participants. Required of senior concentrators; open to other advanced students by permission.

GNSS2001.name: Race, Sex, Capital
GNSS2001.description: Modern sexual fantasies, desires, and subjectivities are indelibly shaped by both the commodity form and the racial legacies of colonialism and chattel slavery. In this interdisciplinary graduate seminar, we will attempt to give greater specificity to this reciprocal “shaping.” How do we think about sexual desires, fantasies, and pleasures? How do they work? Does political economy change their fundamental forms, or merely their symbolic contents? How does erotic life sustain capital flows and racial hierarchies? How can we hope to answer these questions when race, colonialism, and capital have shaped the very conceptual tools that we use to analyze erotic life? We will read widely across history, literary criticism, Black studies, cultural studies, psychoanalysis, and anthropology. Topics include BDSM, interracial sex, sex tourism, and sex work. This is an analogue (i.e., electronic-device free) course.

GNSS2010T.name: Pembroke Research Seminar – The Meanings of Merit
GNSS2010T.description: This seminar will consider how ideas about intellectual value and expertise, in other words, myths of merit, are entangled with divisions of labor and categories of difference. While gender will take a central place in our discussions, we will also explore how the creation of knowledge and the authority to claim it are linked to race, ethnicity, class, and sexuality. We will examine how critiques of merit have shaped work produced in a variety of disciplines and interdisciplinary fields. Our discussions will explore how different fields conceptualize value and expertise in the context of larger, synthetic discussions about questions of merit. We will draw on work from a range of fields in the humanities, social sciences, and sciences. We will engage with an interdisciplinary array of critical scholarship, as well as works of literature, film, visual art, and performance.

GNSS2720.name: Graduate Independent Study
GNSS2720.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Instructor's permission required.

GNSSXLIST.name: Courses of Interest to Concentrators in Gender and Sexuality Studies

GREK0100.name: Essentials of the Greek Language
GREK0100.description: This is the first part of a two-semester Ancient Greek course. The purpose of the course is to develop students’ ability to read and understand Ancient Greek literary texts and to build firm foundations in terms of grammar, vocabulary and reading skills. Selections from Attic Greek authors. No previous knowledge of Greek is required.

GREK0300.name: Introduction to Greek Literature
GREK0300.description: Introduction to Greek literature through intensive reading. Prerequisite: GREK 0200, GREK 0110, or the equivalent. This course focuses on translation and comprehension of Classical Greek prose. The goal is to expand your vocabulary, increase your ease with morphology, and deepen your understanding of syntax as each of these elements of the language interact with each other. The primary text will be Plato’s Apology, with some additional readings by Xenophon.

GREK1010.name: Introduction to Greek Drama
GREK1010.description: Both for students who have recently finished GREK 0300 and 0400 and for those who have little or no experience of translating Greek drama. Begins with a brief review of Attic grammar with readings in Plato. Then turns to Greek drama with students reading a play of one of the dramatists and focusing on philological analysis and meters.

GREK1110I.name: Selections from Greek Authors:  Thucydides
GREK1110I.description: Selected readings, in Ancient Greek, from Thucydides’ History of the Peloponnesian War.

GREK1150.name: Greek Prose Composition
GREK1150.description: Survey of Greek grammar and an opportunity to reflect on problems of translation. Main goals: to improve the students' command of prose syntax (both in reading and writing), and to develop a keen sensitivity towards issues of translation. A variety of texts written in Attic prose are read and analyzed in class. Students are expected to write two to three compositions a week in good Attic prose. Advanced knowledge of ancient Greek is a prerequisite for this course.

GREK1910.name: Special Topics
GREK1910.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

GREK1990.name: Conference: Especially for Honors Students
GREK1990.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

GREK2110A.name: Homer
GREK2110A.description: A close reading of the entire Odyssey, exploring all aspects of the poem, from its oral composition, language, and style to its background myths and social dimensions. Homer's text will be read in Greek, and extensive secondary sources in several languages will be used.

GREK2970.name: Preliminary Exam Preparation
GREK2970.description: For graduate students who have met the tuition requirement and are paying the registration fee to continue active enrollment while preparing for a preliminary examination.

GREK2980.name: Reading and Research

GREK2990.name: Thesis Preparation
GREK2990.description: For graduate students who have met the residency requirement and are continuing research on a full time basis.

GRMN0100.name: Beginning German
GRMN0100.description: A course to learn the German language and about the culture of German-speaking countries. For students interested in gaining a deeper understanding of German history, philosophy, literature, art, music and business through knowledge of the German language. Helps prepare for internships and study abroad, may introduce you to the language of your heritage or to a totally new language, positions you well for further language study, research or other opportunities. 4 hours per week.  No previous knowledge of German required.

GRMN0300.name: Intermediate German I
GRMN0300.description: Focuses on deepening students' understanding of modern German culture by reading texts and viewing films pertinent to Germany today. Intended to provide a thorough review of German grammar and help students develop their writing, reading, listening, and speaking skills. Recommended prerequisite: GRMN 0200.

GRMN0500F.name: Twentieth-Century German Culture
GRMN0500F.description: A broad exploration of twentieth-century German culture using many kinds of written and visual texts (e.g. literature, journalism, film, art). While continuing to work on all four language skills (speaking, listening, reading, writing) students will gain more intensive knowledge about German culture, society, and history. In German. Recommended prerequisite: GRMN 0400.

GRMN0991A.name: Mediated Anxieties, Anxious Mediations (MCM 0903K)
GRMN0991A.description: Interested students must register for MCM 0903K.

GRMN1000B.name: Introduction to German Critical Thought II
GRMN1000B.description: This course is intended for all Brown students eager to engage in complex pleasure by familiarizing themselves with some of the greatest modern German thinkers and the abiding questions they bring into sharp relief. We will focus on issues of being in the world and the prospect of death; art and politics; language and representation; the relation of capitalism and fascism; and the ambivalent role of technology. Authors to be studied include Heidegger, Bloch, Benjamin, Adorno, Horkheimer, Marcuse, and Arendt. When appropriate, we will also ask our German thinkers to speak a little French, as it were, by discovering connections to certain developments in contemporary French thought (Derrida and others). It is not necessary to have taken “Introduction to German Critical Thought I (Kant to Freud)” to enjoy, and benefit from, this course. In English. Students from diverse fields welcome.

GRMN1321E.name: Classicism and its Discontents:  Goethe and Kleist
GRMN1321E.description: This course explores German Classicism through the productive conflict between Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Heinrich von Kleist. Reading major works by these authors, students examine ideals of harmony, form, and moral education, and the ways Kleist exposes their fractures through violence, contingency, and excess. We situate both authors within debates on Enlightenment reason, aesthetics, politics, and subjectivity, tracing how classical norms are asserted, strained, and undone. Close reading, historical context, and comparative analysis guide discussions of drama, prose, and poetry, revealing Classicism not as consensus, but as a contested field whose tensions shaped modern literature and cultural thought broadly. (in German)

GRMN1341H.name: Language and Translation in 20th Century German-Jewish Thought
GRMN1341H.description: This seminar will discuss selected writings on language and translation theory by German-Jewish 20th century thinkers: Franz Rosenzweig, Martin Buber, Walter Benjamin, Gershom Scholem, and Hannah Arendt as well as their (self-)translations from Hebrew (Rosenzweig, Scholem), Yiddish (Scholem), French (Benjamin), and English (Arendt). The seminar will close with a discussion of Paul Celan’s Meridian speech. The guiding questions will be: What role does the Jewish tradition and experience play in those thinkers’ thought on language and translation before and after the Shoah? Can one speak of a ‘Jewish’ theory of language and translation?   This course will be taught by Max Kade Distinguished Visiting Professor, Caroline Sauter (U of Frankfurt)

GRMN1441T.name: Avant-Garde
GRMN1441T.description: In art, the term avant-garde, coined in the late 19th century, refers to artists, movements, or works that deliberately break with established conventions to push aesthetic & conceptual boundaries, often provoking resistance or controversy precisely because they challenge prevailing ideas, processes, & forms. But what does it do to the avant-garde, a now enduring concept, to become canonical, thus turning its disruptive powers into its own category of aesthetic production, guarded, indeed, from institutional despise, & instead folded into recognition? This seminar traces the complicated history of avant-garde & experimental film from the early twentieth century to the present. Moving across European & global traditions, the course examines how filmmakers have challenged narrative, representation, & the limits of their medium through formal experimentation, material investigation, & political critique. Each week pairs a film w/theoretical & historical texts. In English.

GRMN1441U.name: A Strange Neighborhood: Poetry and Philosophy (COLT 1431N)
GRMN1441U.description: Interested students must register for COLT 1431N.

GRMN1661Q.name: Psychoanalysis, Deconstruction and Other Open Secrets (JUDS 1604)

GRMN1970.description: Independent study on a particular topic related to German culture.  In German or English.  At the discretion of the instructor.  Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

GRMN1990.name: Senior Conference
GRMN1990.description: Special work or preparation of an honors thesis under the direction of a faculty member.   Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

GRMN2663E.name: Eros and Logos: On Desire and Literature
GRMN2663E.description: The seminar deals with the productive tension between erotic desire and linguistic expression, eros and logos. It will trace the structural intimacy between erotic desire and language and endeavor to understand the erotic as an intimate relationship with language (philo-logy, philia of logos). Readings include Plato’s Symposion, Sappho’s poetry, as well as selected texts by Anne Carson, Julia Kristeva, Jacques Lacan, Roland Barthes, Audre Lorde, Hélène Cixous, and Werner Hamacher.  This course will be taught by Max Kade Distinguished Professor Caroline Sauter (U of Frankfurt).

HEBR0100.name: Elementary Hebrew
HEBR0100.description: An introduction to the skills of reading, writing, and conversing in contemporary Israeli Hebrew. Students also read Hebrew texts adapted for their level of Hebrew based on biblical, rabbinic, and modern Hebrew literature, which introduce them to the approaches of Hebrew writers in various periods and to a variety of cultural issues. If registration is closed, please contact the professor and a wait list will be created. This is the first half of a year-long course whose first semester grade is normally a temporary one. Neither semester may be elected independently without special permission. Enrollment limited to 20.

HEBR0300.name: Intermediate Hebrew
HEBR0300.description: Develops the skills of reading, writing, and conversing in contemporary Israeli Hebrew at the intermediate level and of reading Hebrew texts of the biblical, rabbinic, and modern periods (biblical stories, rabbinic legends, modern Hebrew poems, stories, essays, newspaper articles). Discussions and compositions focus on the psychological, cultural, political, and social issues reflected in the Hebrew sources that we study. Prerequisite: HEBR 0200 or equivalent. Enrollment limited to 20. If unable to enroll because of closed registration, please contact the professor and a wait list will be created.

HEBR0500.name: Writing and Speaking Hebrew
HEBR0500.description: Enables students to improve their skills in speaking and writing Hebrew on a variety of topics. Features advanced work on language structure and active language practice in the classroom. Class discussions of Israeli current events draw on Israeli stories, poems, television programs, and films and on the Israeli press. Students also compose essays and stories in Hebrew. Prerequisite: HEBR 0400 or equivalent. Enrollment limited to 20.

HIAA0010.name: A Global History of Art and Architecture
HIAA0010.description: Introduction to the global history of art, architecture and material culture from cave paintings to installation art. The course is both an historical survey as well as an analysis of case study examples. In addition to examining visual strategies of representation, the course explores the varied ways in which art shapes and reflects cultural, social, religious, and political concerns. Weekly one-hour conference required. Limited to 200. A

HIAA0023.name: South Asian Art and Architecture
HIAA0023.description: This course is an introduction to South Asian Art & Architecture, from 2500 BCE until the present, and to Southeast Asian Arts connected to them through religion, trade, or conquest. We will explore a range of media—including architecture, painting, sculpture, textiles, and photography—to ask critical questions about the nature of images and their relationship to emotions, the environment, devotion, politics, performance, and other art forms, like literature, music, and dance. The course will include regular visits to the RISD museum (A)

HIAA0032.name: Art and Architecture of the Roman Empire
HIAA0032.description: How did a small city in central Italy grow to become one of the most powerful empires in history? This course explores the art and architecture produced in ancient Rome from its origins in the 6th century BCE to the fourth century CE. It considers a wide variety of media, including reliefs, freestanding sculpture, architectural monuments, mosaics, wall paintings, and daily-life objets. By exploring the role of art and architecture in the formation and expansion of the Empire, considering the experiences of ancient viewers, the course offers a post-colonial reading of ancient Roman history and culture.  (A)

HIAA0052.name: Copán: Art, Architecture, and Archaeology of an Ancient Maya City
HIAA0052.description: As the Copán River winds through a valley of the same name in modern-day Honduras, it meanders past the ruins of Copán, an ancient Maya city established roughly 1600 years ago. This course takes students on a chronological journey through the dynastic history of Copán, as seen through the lens of the stone monuments, precious materials, hieroglyphic inscriptions, and architectural commissions (tombs, temples, and ballcourts) of each of its rulers. As they do, they will come to understand broader aspects of ancient Maya culture, strategies of power, concepts of history and identity, and the role that art and architecture play in communicating these messages in the ancient and modern worlds. A

HIAA0100.name: Introduction to Architectural Design Studio
HIAA0100.description: The class introduces students to basic tools and strategies in architectural design. A warmup exercise and several design assignments guide students to explore questions about form, function, structure, and light. The semester is devoted to the design of a small house. Students are trained in rigorous, conceptual thinking and graphically and verbally clear pronunciation of consequential design logic. By the end of the semester, the proposed building design is presented in concept diagrams, plans, sections, elevations, and a model. Course is intended for first and second year students. Preference is given to actual and future architecture concentrators. To apply for this class, students are required to submit an override request and a note via CAB to specify their concentration, semester level, and previous applications for this class.  Enrollment limited to 15.

HIAA0140.name: Structural and Architectural Analysis
HIAA0140.description: This course examines in greater detail the importance of materials, structures, and processes in architecture and helps students understand how buildings are made and ‘hold together.’ The students will study key examples in brick, wood, reinforced concrete, and steel, and design a series of small sample structures.

HIAA0190.name: Advanced Design Studio
HIAA0190.description: This double-credit studio course builds on the skills taught in the Introductory and Intermediate Studios and will challenge students to design a more complex building. Urban planning strategies are developed to carefully insert the proposed building into a hybrid, densely populated urban context within a city. Students will be briefed to either design a residential housing project or a large public building. Students will analyze the built environment and character of the site to create contextual building designs that strengthen a neighborhood. The final presentation will require a complete set of drawings, renderings, a shared urban context model, and a large-scale model of the proposed building design. A jury of invited architects and professors will conduct a discussion of each project in an exhibition-like setting at the List Art Center. This course can be repeated once for credit.

HIAA1049.name: Art Criticism Workshop
HIAA1049.description:
This seminar broaches the how and why of art criticism: how it is written and why it is undertaken at all. We will investigate the ways in which well written art criticism brings readers into deep relation with visual artwork, and into a dialogue with the histories, values, and concerns that undergird its making. We will examine how criticism provides a window through which we can examine ourselves and our cultural ideals, locating ourselves along the axes of our collective fears, desires, and ambitions.
Learning goals consist of absorbing how to employ the methods and tools needed to produce writing that renders a judgment regarding the historical, aesthetic, intellectual, emotional, cultural, or even financial value of a work of art.

HIAA1152.name: Worldmaking Across the Colonial Sphere: Art and Knowledge in the Spanish Empire
HIAA1152.description: Between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries, the Spanish Americas became a terrain where objects, images, people, and ideas from Europe, Africa, and Asia intersected, and remade one another under the pressures of local practices and demands. This seminar reconsiders the patterns and fluxes of artistic and intellectual circulation in the early modern period from the vantage point of colonial spaces, considered as generative centers of worldmaking. At the center of the seminar stands an eighteenth-century desk and bookcase from Puebla in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston—a European furniture type reimagined through Asian pictorial vocabularies and Indigenous cartographic models to depict a local landscape populated by African subjects. This object serves as case study and methodological guide: a material site where global circulation, artisanal labor, racial representation, and epistemic ordering converged.

HIAA1171.name: Cities, Landscapes, and Design in the Age of Pandemics
HIAA1171.description: This is a course about design and public health. Over the course of the semester, we will examine design proposals by architects, landscape architects, and urban planners which respond to a range of concerns about public space and public health. As a part of our study, we will explore topics including urban planning, and policy strategies proposed by Olmsted, Howard, Burnham, le Corbusier to address to fears about urban density, immigration, and contagion; the effect of treatment protocols for infectious diseases like tuberculosis (hygiene, fresh air, sunlight) on the evolution of the work of designers including Aalto, Neutra, Eames, and others.

HIAA1202.name: Mountains and Waters: Art and Ecology in East Asia
HIAA1202.description:
For more than a millennium, painters and poets across East Asia have acclaimed soaring peaks astride expansive rivers as the most sublime of all subjects. Often termed “landscape” in modern English, these images of “mountains and waters” (shanshui) offer fascinating insights into the ways in which what we now call “the environment” was conceptualized in premodern East Asia. Drawing upon recent eco-aesthetic perspectives, this seminar examines these celebrated monuments of East Asian painting as ecological entities, investigating their relationships with the human and nonhuman beings that participated in their reproduction, and interrogating the moral implications of their enduring appeal. 
First year seminar

HIAA1433.name: Plunder, Wonder, and War:  Histories of Collecting in Sweden, 1500-1700
HIAA1433.description: In this course, we will examine how Sweden waged war, looted art and cultivated wonder to define itself as a modern European state, 1500-1700. Through the lens of museum studies and histories of collecting, we will ask, how does an often-overlooked Nordic perspective complicate our understandings of a “Renaissance”? Sweden’s early modern period is marked by politically motivated art collecting by the House of Vasa (1523-1648), from “father of the nation” Gustav Vasa to the eccentric Philosopher-Queen Christina. Exploring Sweden’s colonial ambitions, developing military infrastructure, and resulting plunder, we will consider how power is buttressed and imaged by material culture.

HIAA1851.name: Staging the World on One Single Spot! Architectural Enquiries into World’s Fairs: London to Osaka
HIAA1851.description: From the mid-19th century to the present, “World’s Fairs” have been spectacular public events. Conceived as temporary showcases of exhibiting host nations, they remained unsurpassed in their staging efforts and are today unique contemporary documents to understand modern-time nation-and-culture building processes in a globalizing world. In this seminar we aim to investigate World's Fairs as temporary playgrounds “to stage the world” by analyzing exhibitions in Europe, North America, Asia and the Arab world. We will unfold our critical enquiry along a threefold analysis about a) the politically motivated motto and the overarching exhibition concept of the hosting nation, b) the spatial organization as image carrier of the exhibition and the architectural form of the theme, the participating countries and their national and and regional pavilions, and c) the social, lively display through opening events, cultural shows and educational schemes. A

HIAA1888.name: Exhibition as Medium
HIAA1888.description: This seminar will examine “the exhibition” as a medium for artists in the modern and contemporary period, with particular focus on developments since the 1960s. We will look at artists who have staged alternative exhibitions in non-traditional spaces, worked within museums and galleries to dismantle curatorial conventions, and, most of all, created exhibitions that stand alone as single works of art. Emphasis will be on the relationship between form and content, the definition of audience and the public, and the intersections and tensions between art and history.

HIAA1920.name: Individual Study Project in the History of Art and Architecture
HIAA1920.description: Reading and reports on an approved topic, supervised by a member of the staff. Project proposals must be submitted and approved no later than the first week of the semester. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HIAA1990.name: Honors Thesis
HIAA1990.description: The subject of the thesis and program of study will be determined by the needs of the individual student. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HIAA1992A.name: HIAA Honors Thesis Workshop
HIAA1992A.description: The Honors Thesis Workshop is a two-semester workshop (offered in the fall and spring semesters) for students writing an Honors Thesis in the History of Art and Architecture, and Architecture concentrations. Students taking the course must also register for HIAA 1990 Honors Thesis with their advisor. This workshop will supplement the work with the advisor by supporting students in research and writing methods, bibliographic practice, archival strategies, and oral presentations. As a cohort, students will do peer reviews and respond to supportive feedback on their thesis. The workshop meets once per week, allowing a second day each week to meet with advisors, the Workshop professor, or peers. Students will submit a draft by the end of the fall term, complete the thesis in spring and present their research to the department at the end of the year.

HIAA2301.name: Finding the Viewer: The Reception of Ancient Art and Architecture
HIAA2301.description:
This graduate seminar will explore the role of viewers in the creation of meanings for ancient art and architecture. The perspectives of the makers of a work of art, patrons and artists, tend to get greater attention in art historical inquiries, in large part because those agents leave more visible traces in the literary and material records. Yet the agency of viewers, although less apparent, can be recovered through careful examination of diverse types of evidence—textual, archaeological, visual—and by relying on viewer-centered theoretical models such as phenomenology and
reception theory. A

HIAA2920.name: Methods of Research and Art Historical Interpretation
HIAA2920.description: Required of first-year and second year history of art and architecture A.M./Ph.D. students. Enrollment limited to 12. Instructor permission required.
