HISP0100.name: Basic Spanish
HISP0100.description: This fast-paced beginning course provides a solid foundation in the development of communicative skills in Spanish (speaking, listening comprehension, reading, writing) as well as insight on the cultures of the Spanish-speaking world. Individual work outside of class (averaging one hour/day) prepares students for in-class activities focused on authentic communication. Placement: students who have never taken Spanish, or scored below 280 on the Brown Placement Exam. Students who have taken Spanish before must take the Brown Placement Exam and check Placement/Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces open at the start of the semester for incoming students. Pre-enrolled students must attend the first four days of class to maintain registered status; notify the instructor in advance of absences in this period.

HISP0200.name: Basic Spanish
HISP0200.description: A continuation of HISP 0100, focusing on acquisition of communicative skills (speaking, listening comprehension, reading, writing) as well as cultural awareness. With successful completion of the course students can carry on short spontaneous conversations and comprehend and produce simple texts involving everyday topics (such as modern day life and its pressures, health, art and culture, nature and the environment, relationships) with good command of grammar and sentence structure. Individual work outside of class (averaging one hour/day) prepares students for in-class activities focused on authentic communication. An additional conversation section (one hour/week) is required. Placement: HISP 0100, Brown placement score of 281 - 380. Students should check Placement/Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at the start of the semester.

HISP0300.name: Intermediate Spanish I
HISP0300.description: This course carries on the work initiated in HISP0100-0200 to develop and strengthen students' linguistic, communicative, academic, and multicultural competencies through content- and language- integrated instruction. This course is framed by an inclusive perspective on learning and embraces diverse identities and communities in the Hispanic World. It offers a variety of texts, themes, and topics related to students’ academic and life experiences, while also helping them develop professional skills. An additional conversation section (one hour/week) is required. Prerequisites: HISP 0200. Brown placement score: 381-460. Students should check Placement and Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies Website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces are available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at the start of the semester.

HISP0400.name: Intermediate Spanish II
HISP0400.description: A continuation of HISP 0300. This course continues to strengthen students’ linguistic, communicative, and multicultural competencies through content- and language- integrated instruction. Students engage with a variety of social, cultural, and personal themes, using language in meaningful, real-world contexts. Emphasis is placed on active engagement, collaborative projects, and interactive activities that enhance both language proficiency and cultural awareness. An additional conversation section (one hour/week) is required. Prerequisites: HISP 0300, Brown placement score: 461-540. Students should check Placement and Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies Website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces are available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at the start of the semester.

HISP0500A.name: Advanced Spanish. Voces jóvenes: Youth in the Spanish-Speaking World
HISP0500A.description: Courses at the 500 level advance students’ Spanish language skills through engagement with a wide range of authentic materials (literary and non-fiction texts, film, podcasts, and more), preparatory individual work for class discussion, and projects completed outside of class, while expanding and refining knowledge of the Spanish language system. HISP0500A focuses on the lived experience of youth, exploring diverse perspectives, experiences and challenges of young people in the Spanish-speaking world, including Latinx communities in the US. Topics include identity, beliefs and values, cultural expression, relationships and technology, among others. An additional conversation section (one hour/week) is required. HISP 0400, Brown placement test score 541-650. Check Placement and Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at start of semester.

HISP0500B.name: Advanced Spanish: Salud y bienestar en comunidad
HISP0500B.description: Courses at the 500 level advance students’ Spanish language skills through engagement with a wide range of authentic materials (literary and non-fiction texts, film, podcasts, and more), preparatory individual work for class discussion, and projects completed outside of class, while expanding and refining their knowledge of the Spanish language system. HISP0500B focuses on Spanish language use in health and wellness contexts, exploring cultural perspectives, common practices, and strategies for communicating effectively about health. Students examine how health and wellness are understood in Spanish-speaking communities and develop linguistic skills needed to engage in meaningful, culturally informed interactions promoting healthier outcomes. HISP 0400, Brown placement test score 541-650. Check Placement and Course Description in the Undergraduate Program section of the Hispanic Studies website. Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at start of semester.

HISP0550.name: Spanish for Heritage Speakers
HISP0550.description:
Heritage speakers of Spanish are students who understand and speak Spanish to some degree, who primarily learned it in their home or community. This course is designed to validate, strengthen and expand the previous linguistic and cultural knowledge these students bring to the classroom. Through a variety of authentic materials, students will explore issues of identity, linguistic rights, equality, and social justice, while developing their Spanish range to include formal registers, and honing their oral communication, reading and writing skills.
Enrollment limited to 15; 12 spaces are available during pre-registration, 3 additional spaces available at the start of the semester. Instructor permission required.

HISP0610N.name: Stories of Nature
HISP0610N.description: What is nature? Are humans part of it or outside it? How has this boundary diverged over time and space, and how has it been expressed? This seminar tackles these questions by exploring stories of nature from various epistemic traditions, with a focus on the Spanish-speaking world. Through ten case studies, we will investigate how the human-nonhuman boundary has been conveyed through storytelling in creation myths, fiction, natural histories, film, and artistic creations. Methodologically, we will survey how scholars have reflected on this boundary from literary, animal and Indigenous studies, while learning to write stories of nature of our own.

HISP0650.name: Advanced Spanish Through Literature & Film
HISP0650.description: HISP 0650 studies literature and film from Latin America and Spain through critical reading and analytical writing. The course serves as an introduction to the literatures and cultures of the Spanish-speaking world, covering a range of periods and genres (e.g. the short story, the novel, poetry, theater, film, and non-fiction). Beyond offering a historical and contextualized panorama of cultural production from the Spanish-speaking world, HISP 0650 will also help you develop new strategies for reading, writing, and thinking about literature and film, preparing you for more advanced literature and culture courses at the 1000 level. Placement: Two HISP courses at the 500 level; HISP 600; or Brown Placement test score of 651 or above.

HISP0750Z.name: Science (in) Fiction
HISP0750Z.description: Science fiction has been called the realism of our time. And Latin America has an exceptionally long history of pushing the bounds of what can be considered to be real. This course examines science fiction in Latin America and the Spanish-speaking world: from early extra-terrestrial travel stories – to the moon and planets beyond – all the way to contemporary hope punk and the creative reimagination of earthly futures. Breaking with the standard tropes of the Global North, Latin American genres of science fiction operate at the intersection of technological skepticism, decolonial inquiry, and multispecies worldmaking. Students will explore how Latin American science fiction writers, filmmakers, and graphic artists – most of them women – interrogate ecological crises, patriarchal paradigms, and the impact of emerging technologies on what it means to be human. Conducted in Spanish.

HISP1240P.name: Health and Medicine in Cervantes and His World (Literature and Science)
HISP1240P.description: This course will explore the vibrant dialogue between literary, medical, and scientific texts of the Classical, Medieval, and Renaissance periods. Focusing on Miguel de Cervantes, alongside a selection of his contemporaries, we will study how premodern ideas of the body and embodiment, disability, illness, healing, and medical authority were represented and (re)negotiated during the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries. We will cover a range of genres, particularly fiction, theater, and treatises to situate literary works within their historical, cultural, scientific, and medical contexts. This will help reveal how premodern writers discuss physical and mental health, patients versus medical “authorities,” individual and public health, etc., while also positioning Cervantes and Early Modern Spanish Literature at the crux of dynamic premodern discourses about the body, health, and the healing potential of medicine.

HISP1331T.name: 'Nuestra parte de noche':  Literatura latinoamericana de lo cruel, macabro y sobrenatural
HISP1331T.description: Prepare to embark on a hair-raising journey through Latin American macabre, supernatural, and horror fiction, spanning short stories and novels from the 19th to the 21st centuries. From ancestral Indigenous legends to contemporary narratives, and from graveyards and haunted dwellings to grim urban landscapes, the course examines how obscure fiction intersects with histories of inequality, human rights abuse, and patriarchal, racist, and capitalist violence. Through close readings of key authors and texts, students will gain a deeper understanding of the literary traditions that have shaped representations of fear, the supernatural, and the uncanny in Latin American literature. Taught in Spanish.

HISP1371R.name: Detention and Freedom in the Americas
HISP1371R.description: On a continent where pretexts for the privation of liberty range from criminal activity to political beliefs to cross-border migration, creative writing - as Chilean-American writer and human rights activist Ariel Dorfman once commented - has a powerful relationship to hope and survival.  In this course, we will read poetry, short fiction and testimonial writing from spaces of detention across Latin America and the U.S., asking how subjects in detention represent themselves, their aspirations to freedom, their physical and social environment, and the languages of defense and protection that ostensibly justify their detention.  Primary texts by contemporary writers in Cuba, Mexico, Argentina, the U.S. and at the Guantánamo Bay Naval Base; readings and class discussion in Spanish.

HISP1602C.name: Desire in Iberian Cinema
HISP1602C.description: How does desire shape national cinemas? What is the relationship between an individual’s desire and what they see on screen? What are the dynamics of desire in the cinematic screen? Through films ranging from the late nineteenth century to contemporary productions, this course examines, in Spanish and Portuguese cinema, how desire is constructed, repressed, performed, or liberated, and how Iberian filmmakers engage with themes such as colonialism and imperialism, dictatorship and democracy, memory, censorship, queerness, bodily autonomy, and transgression, and national imaginaries. Combining film theory with cultural and gender studies, the course invites students to consider how desire becomes a site of resistance, vulnerability, and creativity within the evolving landscapes of Iberian cinema. Students will gain tools for film analysis while considering broader cultural and aesthetic questions that shape Iberian cinema.

HISP1980.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HISP2350M.name: Poetics of the Avant-Garde in Latin America
HISP2350M.description: This course traces the shocks and flows of avant-garde activities through Latin America in the early twentieth century and beyond. We will explore manifestoes, poetry, artworks, and film from Argentina, the Caribbean, Chile, Brazil, Mexico, and Peru, looking at the ways in which avant-garde writing and art engages the senses to produce local forms for local contexts, but also to communicate beyond them. We will also look at the avant-garde’s afterlives in the 1970s and the early 2000s. Some of the questions we will ask are: what are the distinctive forms and concerns of Latin American modernity, and how do these differ from European aesthetic politics? What kind of regional network gets activated by the historical avant-gardes, and what is that network’s relation to global flows? How and why does the avant-garde reappear in later moments, and to what ends?

HISP2620Q.name: Gender and the Body in Modern Spain
HISP2620Q.description: This course explores Spanish cultural production from the nineteenth century to the present, using gender and the body as axes of exploration and analysis. It examines representations of gender roles and norms, as well as their subversion and critique, in a variety of works, including novels, films, and essays. The course readings, which combine a literary and/or filmic text with key critical and theoretical selections, move chronologically and cover a wide range of topics such as: the connections between modernity, capitalism, and gender identity; the development of feminism and persistence of misogyny, patriarchal structures, and machismo; relationships between gender, politics, and violence; biopolitics and medical discourse; gender/queer/trans activism and calls for recognition and rights, among many others. Throughout, we will interrogate the social and cultural production and representation of gendered bodies, subjects, and subjectivities.

HISP2990A.name: Learning & Teaching Spanish as a Foreign Language
HISP2990A.description: This course provides practicing and prospective teachers of Spanish as a second language (L2) with an introduction to the field of second language acquisition (SLA) and its application to language teaching methodology and pedagogy, with a specific focus on the teaching of Spanish. In addition to the theoretical discussion, there is a significant practical component to the course so you can start (or continue) to develop skills and materials for your own work as an instructor at Brown University and beyond.

HISP2991.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HIST0150A.name: History of Capitalism
HIST0150A.description: Capitalism didn't just spring from the brain of Adam Smith. Its logic is not encoded on human DNA, and its practices are not the inevitable outcome of supply and demand. So how did capitalism become the dominant economic system of the modern world? History can provide an answer by exploring the interaction of culture and politics, technology and enterprise, and opportunity and exploitation from the era of the slave ship to the era of the container ship. HIST 0150 courses introduce students to methods of historical analysis, interpretation, and argument. This class presumes no economics background, nor previous history courses.

HIST0233.name: Colonial Latin America
HIST0233.description: Colonial Latin America, from Columbus's voyage in 1492 to Independence in the nineteenth century, was the creation of three peoples: Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans. Spanish and Portuguese conquerors brought with them the world of the Crusades, the Inquisition, and the Renaissance. Native Americans lived there already, in rich empires and hunter-gatherer bands. Africans came as slaves from Senegal, Nigeria, Congo and Angola, bringing old traditions and creating new ones. These diverse peoples blended together to form a new people. This was a place of violence, slavery and oppression -- but also of art, faith, new societies, new ideas. P

HIST0252.name: The American Civil War
HIST0252.description: This course, covering the period roughly from 1820-1865 and focusing mostly on 1860-1865, examines the origins of the Civil War, the war itself, and preliminary efforts at reconstruction during wartime. The class meetings and readings will focus on the transformation wrought by the war, investigating in particular certain issues relevant to current affairs: 1) enslavement, emancipation, and struggles for equality; 2) sectionalism, secession, and insurrection; 3) the role of law in the prosecution and resolution of war; and 4) the role of the Civil War in American popular culture and politics. Students should consult the course syllabus via CAB before registering.

HIST0255.name: African American History From Emancipation to Obama
HIST0255.description: This course is an introductory survey of African American political, cultural, and intellectual history from the late nineteenth century to the very recent past. Through lectures, discussions, and reading of primary and secondary sources, students will become acquainted with the lesser known aspects of African American history and critically re-examine the more famous pivotal moments and movements of the last two hundred years. Topics include citizenship and democratic participation, gender, labor and collective organizing, Black inter/nationalism and the political uses of African American history.

HIST0558C.name: Latinx Social Movement History
HIST0558C.description: This course examines the history of Latinx social movements and politics during the 20th century into the present moment. Students will learn how various Latinx groups have organized around issues of race, ethnicity, labor, class, immigration, sports, gender, sexuality, citizenship, reproductive rights, and education. We will explore how these groups have utilized social and political organizing to make demands for social justice and equality. By utilizing primary and secondary sources, students will explore major questions, theory, and research methods pertinent to the historical narratives of Latinx people. Students will closely examine the legacy of these social movements and their implications for present-day politics and organizing.

HIST0559C.name: Archives and Activism
HIST0559C.description: This U.S. history seminar introduces students to the Brown University Library’s Special Collections by examining its archival holdings on 20th century activism. We will focus on the archives of imprisoned activist Mumia Abu-Jamal, student protest at Brown, and the Hall-Hoag Collection of US right- and left-wing political groups.

HIST0592.name: American Revolution in Popular Culture
HIST0592.description: Catchy dialogue, lovable characters, and unforgettable music have shaped popular understanding of the complexities of American independence. Indeed, college-aged Americans are likely to know their American Revolution primarily through Liberty’s Kids, American Girl dolls, and such musicals as Hamilton and 1776. How do these popular culture representations of the American past work to guide the present and future possibilities of American society? To shape the consciousness of Generation Z? To turn history into commodity, or to mobilize it in the service of radically divergent political agendas? As national attention turns to the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, this class explores the American Revolution’s multiple lives in popular culture since the Bicentennial. Students will read scholarship on the Revolution itself, as well as works on the politics of culture in modern America.

HIST0658D.name: Walden + Woodstock: The American Lives of Ralph Waldo Emerson and Bob Dylan
HIST0658D.description: Emerson and Dylan are cultural icons. Emerson has been called “Mr. America” and Dylan has just won the Nobel Prize for Literature. Both had boundless energy for public performance and self-representation; both actively supported turning points in the civil rights struggle; both raged against American military aggression; both were at the epicenter of a wide circle of intellectuals, while denying their own centrality. What is the celebrity intellectual’s responsibility to society while remaining true to oneself? Poems, essays, autobiographies, songs, and movies provide insight into these eternally fascinating geniuses and their times.

HIST0930L.name: Israel's Wars (JUDS 0050H)
HIST0930L.description: Interested students must register for JUDS 0050H.

HIST0931B.name: An Introduction to Africana Studies (AFRI 0090).
HIST0931B.description: Interested students must register for AFRI 0090.

HIST0931E.name: Pirates, Bandits, Terrorists: Outlaws in the Middle East (MES 0415)
HIST0931E.description: Interested students must register for MES 0415.

HIST0940D.name: The Border/La Frontera(ETHN 0090A)
HIST0940D.description: Interested students must register for ETHN 0090A.

HIST0940P.name: The Meaning of History in the Ancient World (CLAS 0210F)
HIST0940P.description: Interested students must register for CLAS 0210F.

HIST1070.name: Postcolonial Africa
HIST1070.description: How did Africans remake state and society in the wake of empire? Picking up at the end of WWII, this course explores prolonged and varied transitions in postcolonial Africa. A range of political and economic reforms intended to promote authenticity or achieve modernity unfolded under the pressures of the Cold War and the intransigence of white settler societies. By engaging primary sources, we track conversations on Africa’s postcolonial experiments and gauge the effects on the quality of everyday life. Students will find, edit, and comment on primary sources of their own choosing for possible inclusion in a published work.

HIST1121.name: The Modern Chinese Nation: An Idea and Its Limits
HIST1121.description: How did the Chinese empire become a nation-state? This course introduces the history of Chinese societies from 1850, when a massive civil war destabilized the country and sent a new wave of migrants across the globe. We will explore how local and regional society was affected by the spread of new conceptions of the Chinese nation, new kinds of government, and cultural and technological innovations. Coursework addresses the construction of race, ethnicity, and religion as well as gender and sexuality; the effects of war and catastrophe; different formulations of revolution and self-strengthening; and more.

HIST1141.name: Japan in the Age of the Samurai
HIST1141.description: This course is for students interested in exploring Japan’s remarkable cultural, political and social transformations during the Age of the Samurai, which began in the late 12th century and came to a close in the mid-19th century. Lectures, readings and films will explore how the emergence of new forms of military expertise and technologies led to the creation of warrior-led “tent governments,” that first co-existed with and eventually supplanted the structures of power centered on Kyoto and the Imperial Court. Open to all students. P

HIST1202.name: Formation of the Classical Heritage: Greeks, Romans, Jews, Christians, and Muslims
HIST1202.description: Explores essential social, cultural, and religious foundation blocks of Western Civilization, 200 BCE to 800 CE. The main theme is the eternal struggle between universalism and particularism, including: Greek elitism vs. humanism; Roman imperialism vs. inclusion; Jewish assimilation vs. orthodoxy; Christian fellowship vs. exclusion, and Islamic transcendence vs. imminence. We will study how ancient Western individuals and societies confronted oppression and/or dramatic change and developed intellectual and spiritual strategies still in use today. Students should be prepared to examine religious thought from a secular point of view. There is no prerequisite or assumed knowledge of the period. P

HIST1205.name: The Long Fall of the Roman Empire
HIST1205.description: The collapse of the Roman Empire was the crucible in which the cultures of the medieval West, Byzantium, and Islam were forged. This class examines the tensions and transformations within Mediterranean society between 250 and 1100 CE and how these tribulations gave birth to new identities, boundaries, economies, and religious beliefs. We will explore too the points of contact between the emerging Latin, Byzantine, and Islamic worlds and how people living in the late ancient and early medieval Mediterranean sought to devise solutions to the challenges that confronted them as their worlds collapsed, expanded, and changed. Class meetings will interweave narrative and thematic lectures with student analysis of primary sources in translation. Topics include early Christianity, the body, gender, barbarian invasions and the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the rise of Islam, Charlemagne, and the Vikings. P

HIST1242.name: History of the European Union
HIST1242.description: This course offers an introductory survey of the history of the European Union. While the EU itself is only a few decades old, the idea of and desire for European unity date back centuries. We will explore the deeper genealogies of the European idea as well as specific events of the 20th century that led to the creation of the modern EU. We will close by considering more recent events that have shaped the EU since its formal inception in 1993, from EU expansion into East-Central and Southeastern Europe to European states’ involvement in and reaction to the US invasion of Iraq and Afghanistan to Brexit and the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Themes include enlightenment, empire, revolution, nationalism, ideas of federation and confederation, constitutionalism, democracy, Nazism and fascism, state socialism, globalization, migration, military intervention, climate change, and digital technology.

HIST1262M.name: Truth on Trial: Justice in Italy, 1400-1800
HIST1262M.description: Why do we think that one human being can judge another? How did this activity, enshrined in legal and political systems, profoundly shape society?  This course examines the changing face of justice, from the medieval ordeal to judicial torture; the expansion of inquisitorial and state law courts; and the critical role the judicial system played in shaping Italian society. Using Italy as a focus, the course explores how law courts defined social, political, scientific, and religious truth in the early modern period.  P

HIST1382.name: The Environmental History of Latin America
HIST1382.description: This course offers students an introduction to environmental history from perspectives that center the societies and ecologies of Latin America and the Caribbean.  Thinking across different chronologies and spaces, we will draw from a range of historical and interdisciplinary scholarship, as well as primary sources, to examine changing relationships between Latin American environments and their attendant social, cultural, political, urban, agrarian, maritime, legal and economic histories. Our collective explorations on these topics will adopt various scales of analysis, from local and regional to continental, and will push us to approach key themes of Precolonial, Colonial, and Modern Latin American historiography from an environmental lens, including: Indigenous histories; colonialism, extractivism, and slavery; Afro-Latinx histories; capitalism and dependency theory; the politics of modern conservation.

HIST1457A.name: Understanding the Palestinians: 1700-1948
HIST1457A.description: This course draws on new scholarship that centers Palestinian experiences for understanding their transformation from a largely peasant society under Ottoman rule (1516-1917) into a dispossessed and stateless people after the Nakba (catastrophe) of 1948.We explore the emergence of modern Palestinian society in the 18th and 19th centuries, the encounters with European Zionist settlers since the 1880s, and the transformative period of British colonization (1917-1948). Ultimately, we ask: Who are the Palestinians? And what does the Nakbateach us about the making of the modern world? A sequel course (1457B) covering the period from 1948-present, will be offered in the Spring 2027 semester.

HIST1507.name: American Babylon: Crisis and Reckoning in the Postwar United States, 1945-1980
HIST1507.description: This course explores the major cultural and political developments in U.S. history in the tumultuous postwar decades: liberalism, radicalism, and conservatism; race, class, gender, and sexuality in shaping national life; the Cold War and the fate of the New Deal; rise of the New Right; and the making of a second gilded age, among others. We consider postwar history in three broad periods: One, the consolidation of “Cold War liberalism” under international and domestic anticommunism through the 1960s; Two, a period we might call the “second Reconstruction,” between 1954 and 1973, when race-, gender-, and sexuality-based movements produced a social and legal revolution on behalf of equality and human rights; and Three, a period of backlash to the rights revolution that overlapped with the rise of an oligarchic phase of capitalism known as “neoliberalism,” between the 1970s and the present.

HIST1800.name: Religion and Power in North America to 1865
HIST1800.description: This course explores the relationship of various forms of religion and power in North America from the pre-Columbian period through the US Civil War and Reconstruction.  We explore the confluence and conflict of Indigenous, African, and European beliefs and practices.  Topics include: native agency and settler colonialism; race and slavery; war and politics; gender and patriarchy; soul-craft and statecraft; domination and empowerment.

HIST1830B.name: Politics and the Psyche from Sigmund Freud to Donald Trump
HIST1830B.description: This combined lecture/discussion course explores the relation between politics and the emotions from Sigmund Freud’s discovery of the unconscious in Vienna around 1900 to the rise of populist and anti-democratic politics in the United States and Europe today. Historical knowledge generally focuses on civilizations, societies, systems, and events as they move, evolve, and transform through time. Psychoanalytic knowledge added the inner, mental (psychic) lives of people and cultures. Psychoanalysis redefined the humanities, the social sciences, and their relationships, paving the way as well for new approaches such as gender and sexuality studies. We will focus on the role of psychoanalysis as a political science, attuned to the modes of mass and media politics of the 20th and 21st centuries.

HIST1840.name: Popular Culture in the Americas
HIST1840.description: Today, American culture is an object of popular fascination—and, at times, repudiation—all over the world. This course explores how that came to be, as well as the region’s enduring impact on global popular culture. Beginning in the early colonial period and extending through the twenty-first century, the course will cover the emergence of popular and mass cultures across the hemisphere, stretching from Canada to Chile, as well as the transnational connections that have informed their development.

HIST1845.name: How to Do Gay and Lesbian History
HIST1845.description: Taught between the History Dept and the Hay Library, this will uncover queer pasts through engagement with collections held at Brown and visits from experts in the collections and in queer histories. We will ask: how do historians do their work in the field of Gay and Lesbian History? What are their habits, what are their limits, and from which fields do they draw insight? How do they imagine who their research subjects were, especially given that "gay and lesbian" are modern terms? How do curators decide what to include in collections, and go about finding, collecting, and processing those materials? Students can expect to get hands-on practice in the collections at the Hay and will produce a piece of original research as a final project.

HIST1903.name: The Information Age
HIST1903.description: What does it mean to say we live in an “information age”? How did computers become personal and platforms ubiquitous? This lecture-discussion course approaches these and other questions through the entangled histories of computing and communication in the United States. Behind the eccentric innovators and ‘laws’ of manufacturing, we find a social history driven by friction between interest groups—corporations, designers, lawmakers, users—as well as contestation over values like privacy and access. Students will explore methods for analyzing computational artifacts and communications infrastructure alongside more traditional sources, and for reframing conversations about our present using history. Beginning in the age of railroads and telegraphs, we consider the changing role of the state in technological development and regulation, the social and legal construction of the Internet, and the emerging political economy of artificial intelligence—all while keeping people front and center.

HIST1930S.name: Roman History II: The Roman Empire and Its Impact (CLAS 1320)
HIST1930S.description: Interested students must register for CLAS 1320.

HIST1931T.name: Ancient Greek Athletics (CLAS 1450)
HIST1931T.description: Interested students must register for CLAS 1450.

HIST1940A.name: South Africa since 1990
HIST1940A.description: South Africa entered a new era when Nelson Mandela walked out of prison in 1989. Apartheid, the world’s most extreme form of racial segregation ended and the country became a liberal democracy. The exhilaration and disillusionment since then are enormous. With an emphasis on the experiences of ordinary people, especially the most vulnerable Black South Africans, this seminar considers transformation and its limits. We move across disciplines to explore economic precarity, racial and cultural politics, youth activism, public health, and more. Students will participate in weekly discussions, collaborate in creating a public-facing digital resource, and produce a final project.

HIST1950A.name: The Indigenous Worlds of the American Revolution
HIST1950A.description: This course considers the wider era of the American Revolution through the experiences and actions of Indigenous nations. Although the usual story of the American War of Independence is centered on the political conflict between the American colonists and the colonies (and eventual states), the view from Indian country looked vastly different, with divergent allegiances and experiences ranging from 1760 to 1795, during which the American Revolution was only one conflict.

HIST1954F.name: Globalism before Globalization: The Interconnected World of the Early Middle Ages
HIST1954F.description: Long before the internet or digital technology, the world was a globally interconnected place. This class looks at a period usually considered an age of localism, ca. 400–1000 CE, and considers the contacts and cultural exchanges between societies usually studied in isolation, across Afro-Eurasia, Oceania, and the Americas. Class sessions interweave student analysis of primary sources in translation and assessment of modern scholarship. Themes include art and visual culture, world literature, religion, ritual, courtly society, political and social formation, cultural hybridity, trade, disease, voyages of exploration, race-making, and early medieval understandings of human connectedness on a global scale. P

HIST1954S.name: Technology, Data, and the Authoritarian State
HIST1954S.description: The course explores how modern authoritarian regimes use and shape information as a means to power, and how post-authoritarian societies reckon with that information’s legacies. Drawing on global examples (predominantly Europe, Russia and the Soviet Union, and China and elsewhere in Asia) from the 19th to the 21st centuries, topics include information technologies (from filing systems to AI) and their application; mapping, census, and population control; policing and surveillance; historical revisionism; censorship and control of expression; and forms of resistance and dissent. We will also explore the process of transitional justice, including the opening and preservation of records; grassroots and official fact-finding; story telling; judicial reckonings; and ethical questions about who owns and is owed information.

HIST1956F.name: Brazilian Biomes: An Environmental History of Brazil
HIST1956F.description: With stunning and unparalleled ecological diversity, Brazil developed historically in concert with the contours of its natural environments. This seminar explores six regional biomes – from the Atlantic Forest to the Amazon, from the Pampa to the Pantanal–in tracing the social and cultural history of Brazil. Each two-week period focuses on a particular ecology, geography, and temporality, beginning with the early history of the Amazon, passing through Europe’s encounter with the Atlantic rainforest and migratory histories from the arid shrublands of the Caatinga, and ending with the exploitation of mining regions of the Cerrado. Each week we ask: how did the environment fundamentally shape the experience of Brazil’s diverse peoples – Indigenous, African, European, and mestizo – and how were Brazilian historical narratives and literary expressions shaped by these different regional experiences? Knowledge of Portuguese is recommended but not required.

HIST1961O.name: Writing and Power in China's Early Empires
HIST1961O.description: Most of the written texts that have survived from the ancient world were written by powerful men. How can we read them against the grain to reconstruct the world of early Chinese empires and the place of women, the rural majority, and conquered populations within it? This course will analyze literary and archaeological texts primarily from the Han empire (c. 202 BCE-220 BCE) to understand how written texts encode diverse forms of social and political power, and reveal struggles over them. Genres include historiography, poetry, and political and economic texts.  We will also consider how early Chinese writings about imperial conquests, foreigners, gender, and the canonization of the Confucian classics compare to other traditions. P

HIST1962G.name: Southeast Asian Food History
HIST1962G.description: This new course aims to introduce students to Southeast Asian history through the lens of food. Spanning the region, it will examine the economic, cultural, medicinal, and social life of food while considering, too, how food--as method and archive--opens new horizons for the study of Southeast Asian history.

HIST1964A.name: Age of Impostors: Fraud, Identification, and the Self in Early Modern Europe
HIST1964A.description: Alchemists claiming to possess the philosophers' stone; basilisks for sale in the market; Jews pretending to be Catholics; women dressing as men: early modern Europe appeared to be an age of impostors. Officials responded to this perceived threat by hiring experts and creating courts, licenses, passports, and other methods of surveillance in an era before reliable documentation, photography, DNA. And yet one person's fraud was another's self-fashioning. We will examine instances of dissimulation, self-fashioning, and purported fraud, efforts to identify and stem deception, and debates about what was at stake when people and things were not what they seemed. P

HIST1980C.name: Histories of Global Wetlands (ENVS 1915)
HIST1980C.description: Interested students must register for ENVS 1915.

HIST1981T.name: Problems in Islamic Studies: The Latest Methods and Theories in the Study of Islam (RELS 1530H)
HIST1981T.description: Interested students must register for RELS 1530H.

HIST1982B.name: Sex and Society in Modern China (EAST 1307)
HIST1982B.description: Interested students must register for EAST 1307.

HIST1990.name: Undergraduate Reading Courses
HIST1990.description: Guided reading on selected topics. Section numbers vary by instructor. Please check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HIST1992.name: History Honors Workshop for Prospective Thesis Writers
HIST1992.description: Prospective honors students are encouraged to enroll in HIST 1992 during semesters 5 or 6. HIST 1992 offers a consideration of historical methodology and techniques of writing and research with the goal of preparing to write a senior thesis in history.  The course helps students refine research skills, define a project,  and prepare a thesis prospectus, which is required for admission to honors. Students who complete honors may count HIST 1992 as a concentration requirement. Limited to juniors who qualify for the honors program.

HIST1993.name: History Honors Workshop for Thesis Writers, Part I
HIST1993.description: All students admitted to the History Honors Program must enroll in HIST 1993 for two semesters of thesis research and writing. They may enroll in the course during semesters 6 and 7, or 7 and 8. Course work entails researching, organizing, writing a history honors thesis. Presentation of work and critique of peers' work required. Limited to seniors and juniors who have been admitted to History Honors Program. HIST 1993 is a mandatory S/NC course. See History Concentration Honors Requirements.

HIST1994.name: History Honors Workshop for Thesis Writers, Part II
HIST1994.description: This is the second half of a year-long course, upon completion the grade will revert to HIST 1993. Prerequisite: HIST 1993.

HIST2890.name: Preliminary Examination Preparation
HIST2890.description: For graduate students who have met the tuition requirement and are paying the registration fee to continue active enrollment while preparing for a preliminary examination.

HIST2910.name: Reading and Research
HIST2910.description: Section numbers vary by instructor. Please see check Banner for the correct section number and CRN to use when registering for this course.

HIST2920.name: History Now
HIST2920.description: Focused on current trends in historical writing and research, with emphasis on presenting a diverse range of cutting-edge work in historical and historiographical context. Required for all first-year PhD students in History.

HIST2940.name: Writing History
HIST2940.description: Required of all 3rd semester Ph.D. students.

HIST2970K.name: Graduate Readings in Atlantic World
HIST2970K.description: This course is a wide-ranging readings course in the field of Atlantic World History. Readings will consider the full range of empires and peoples of the wider Atlantic basin, including Africans, Native Americans, and Europeans, in the period spanning the fifteenth and nineteenth centuries. Special attention will be given to wider oceanic and global trends in the field, including its relationship to historiographies on Colonial Latin America, the African Diaspora, and Early America. All graduate students welcome.

HIST2971J.name: Topics in 19th c. U.S. History
HIST2971J.description: This state-of-the-field course will introduce students to nineteenth-century U.S. history, with specific attention to how recent transnational, imperial, institutional, and cultural approaches have reframed older debates over the "Age of Jackson," "Manifest Destiny," and the "Market Revolution." This seminar offers core readings for students preparing a comprehensive exam field, while providing others with content knowledge to teach this period of American history.

HIST2982C.name: Women and the History of Sexuality
HIST2982C.description: This thematic seminar will prepare PhD students for research and teaching in the fields of women's history and the history of sexuality. The class is shaped by three lines of inquiry: first, we will position the category "woman" as a question, asking, for example, how ideas about race and class have shaped that category across time and place. Second, we will follow select lines of historical inquiry that begin with "woman" as well as "sex" "sexuality" and "gender" (topics include histories of the family, reproduction, violence, state and governance, aesthetics, feminism). Finally, we will trace the intertwined historiographic and institutional co-evolutions of the fields of women's history, the history of sexuality, and gay and lesbian history. While this class is concerned primarily with history, students will gain some limited exposure to key texts in feminist theory.

HIST2990.name: Thesis Preparation
HIST2990.description: For graduate students who have met the residency requirement and are continuing research on a full time basis.

HIST2991.name: History Dissertation Writing Workshop
HIST2991.description: This seminar is for History PhD students in residence at Brown who are post-exams and are at any stage of writing their dissertations. It is intended to support dissertators by providing a structured community for setting and sharing goals, writing, and discussing chapters-in-progress. It meets every other week and is a half credit S/NC course.

HIST2992K.name: The Politics of Knowledge (STS 2000)
HIST2992K.description: Interested students must register for STS 2000.

HIST2992N.name: Popular Science (HMAN 2402M)
HIST2992N.description: Interested students must register for HMAN 2402.

HIST2992O.name: Nonhuman-Inhuman: Readings on the Boundaries of Humanity (HMAN 2402O)
HIST2992O.description: Interested students must register for HMAN 2402O.

HMAN0800B.name: The Art of International Relations
HMAN0800B.description: From the ritual handshakes of country leaders to iconic photographs of migrants and refugees, from the use of music in combat and torture to the mobilization of art to make a better world, aesthetics informs the way international actors present themselves, portray the world, perceive others, and conceive of peace, conflict, and war. At the intersection of the humanities and social sciences, this course explores cultural practices constitutive of the diplomatic stage, international society, transnational networks, globalization, and postcoloniality in the 20th and 21st centuries. These include theatre, literature, music, dance, images, film, television, and social media.

HMAN0900Y.name: Copán: Art, Architecture, and Archaeology of an Ancient Maya City (HIAA 0052)
HMAN0900Y.description: Interested students must register for HIAA 0052.

HMAN0901.name: Writing Black School Futures: Advanced Topics in the Cultural History of Black Education
HMAN0901.description: This interdisciplinary seminar invites students to explore the possibilities of more equal and affirming schools through the study of Black education’s past. Using novels, biographies, film, essays, and other primary and secondary historical accounts, we will explore the problems and possibilities of education as told through 20th-century Black cultural works. We will consider the following questions: Why and how has education been central to the political, economic, and cultural production of Black communities? How do these cultural productions describe a vision for education in the historic moment under study? And how might they offer new epistemologies to think beyond what we know and push us toward alternative educational praxis? Our historic investigation will encompass the antebellum and post-antebellum eras, the Harlem Renaissance, and the Civil Rights era, and will extend into the contemporary moment.

HMAN1000A.name: The Cogut Institute for the Humanities Research Seminar
HMAN1000A.description: This yearlong seminar involves reading and discussing in-progress research by the annual fellows of the Cogut Institute for the Humanities, an interdisciplinary group of faculty, postdoctoral fellows, graduate students, and undergraduates engaged in extended research on a major project or honors thesis. Students read a wide range of works-in-progress, prepare questions and participate in seminar discussions, serve as first questioners for specific sessions assigned to them in advance, and present their own work twice during the year. Students are required to complete both semesters (HMAN 1000A in the fall and HMAN 1000B in the spring) to receive credit. Admission to the course requires that students have received the Cogut Institute Undergraduate Fellowship for the year in which they enroll. More information about the fellowship and application process may be found at https://humanities.brown.edu/apply/undergraduate-fellowship.

HMAN1201.name: Blue Humanities, Black Humanities
HMAN1201.description: Water is a central theme in Black queer ecological thought. It is at once a metaphor, a method, and a material condition for lives shaped and lost by oceanic crossings. In this course, oceanic spaces will become our laboratories for understanding Black queer sociality, gender, and sexuality. We will turn to critical thinkers who grapple with the depths of the sea. For example, we will contemplate how water floods Dionne Brand’s memory as she searches for the “Door of No Return.” We will also examine the unflinching manner in which Christina Sharpe charts the wake, tracing what water erases. Additionally, we will discuss Alexis Pauline Gumbs’s poetic breath as she breathes with marine mammals. Ultimately, we will explore a wide range of literature, poetry, and visual culture to understand what “endures” after maritime encounters.

HMAN1201A.name: Oceanic Methods, Archipelagic Thinking, and Tidal Ethnographies
HMAN1201A.description: This seminar makes critical and urgent connections across environmental humanities and ethnographic methods through an archipelagic, and thus relational, mode of thinking. Blue humanities help us to think with the oceanic as a metaphor of connectivity. Beyond metaphor, we will be experimenting with the oceanic as a response to mobility and environmental change. How does the warming ocean shape the meaning and temporalities of risk? What methods are suitable in attending to shifting oceans that carry traces of refusal and survival? We will approach these questions through film, fiction, and poetry, as well as ethnographies of oceanic connections that strive to map this extremely dynamic site. This intersectional approach invites students to think beyond the oceanic space as an ontological other, and posits the oceanic mobilities as connecting tissue between resistance and survival.

HMAN1300B.name: Introduction to Spatial Digital Humanities
HMAN1300B.description: The spatial humanities merges geographical information systems (GIS), geospatial analysis, and quantitative data with critical questions in the humanities and areas of study such as literature, history, art, and culture. It asks the “why” in the “where” in digital humanities (DH). This course introduces students to the digital and virtual worlds of maps, data, algorithms, VR/AR/XR, and critical DH scholarships. Together, we approach the spatial humanities from a variety of angles, including race, gender, de/anti/postcolonialism, and other subfields in DH. Students will experiment with prominent digital tools (Omeka Neatline, Leaflet, ArcGIS, StoryMaps, etc.) to develop their digital skillsets and learn to create maps and spatial artifacts of their own.

HMAN1977E.name: The Common Good: Past, Present, and Future
HMAN1977E.description: While many endorse the ideal of serving the “common good,” far fewer agree on what the pursuit of that ideal involves. This has been the case for millennia, as various philosophical, ethical, and religious traditions have named the common good and similar concepts as objectives to guide human behavior. This course examines interpretations of this ideal and its implications, asking what the common good has been, is now, and might yet be. Exploring histories, cultures, and economic systems within and beyond the United States, in contemporary and ancient contexts, students will consider how conflicting visions of the common good have animated debates around such diverse social phenomena as political systems, labor unions, religious communities, tax and welfare policies, and rules for Facebook groups and other virtual communities. Probing these debates, students will refine their understandings of their own common goods.

HMAN1977H.name: Critical Race Theory Now
HMAN1977H.description: Moving beyond the reductive and polarizing deployment of Critical Race Theory (CRT) in current political discourse, this interdisciplinary seminar traces its history as a legal intervention foregrounding race and racism in the development of U.S. law and in the (infra)structures of U.S. civic, socioeconomic, and political life. Together, we will explore the central tenets of CRT, including the ubiquity and permanence of racism, intersectionality, whiteness as property and currency, and redistributive justice. Reading seminal texts of CRT alongside contemporary African American literature, we will attend to specific topics, such as affirmative action, immigration, mass incarceration, and reparations. The overarching inquiry of this course is: (1) how might the law be complicit in upholding racial hierarchy as well hierarchies of gender, class, sexuality, and citizenship, and (2) how might the law and literature be used to dismantle those same hierarchies?

HMAN1977U.name: The Theater of Musical Performance
HMAN1977U.description: Taking approaches from performance studies, media studies, historical musicology, and cultural studies, this course seeks to discover aspects of musical ritual, audience experience, and identity construction that have become transparent or normalized by their familiarity. We will explore the visual and theatrical dimensions of music performances through analysis of live performances, video clips, photographs, and other historical documents such as oral histories and criticism. After an initial two weeks of focused theoretical reading, students will launch research projects based on genres and artists of their own choice and give periodic updates on their research progress. The regular syllabus concentrates on the kinds of music that have received the most extensive and insightful scholarly treatment, and on readings by scholars such as Philip Auslander, Fabian Holt, Daphne Brooks, and Martha Feldman who have probed questions of musical performance most ambitiously.

HMAN1978A.name: The Philosophy of AI (PHIL 1835)
HMAN1978A.description: Interested students must register for PHIL 1835.

HMAN1978B.name: Avant-Garde (GRMN 1441T)
HMAN1978B.description: Interested students must register for GRMN 1441T.

HMAN1978C.name: Buddhism and the Body (CLAS 1165)
HMAN1978C.description: Interested students must register for CLAS 1165.

HMAN1978E.name: The Information Age (HIST 1903)
HMAN1978E.description: Interested students must register for HIST 1903.

HMAN2301.name: Digital Humanities Capstone Seminar
HMAN2301.description: Participants in the Digital Humanities Capstone Seminar will learn how to design and build their own digital humanities project and/or participate as a key member on an already established digital humanities project with a faculty leader through hands-on, step by step instruction. Students will grapple with key methodologies and theoretical frameworks (including critical, Black, Indigenous, and Latinx digital humanities) and consider how to situate their own work within these ideas. Seminar participants will participate in the Digital Humanities Salon, where they will also present their project. Where desired and advisable, the capstone project may build toward dissertation work. Admission in the course is conditional on enrollment in the doctoral certificate in digital humanities, and partial or full completion of the digital tools and methods requirement.

HMAN2401L.name: Postcolonial Theory (ENGL 2900X)
HMAN2401L.description: Interested students must register for ENGL 2900X.

HMAN2402M.name: Popular Science
HMAN2402M.description: Science has often been depicted as a subject produced by experts, then transmitted to the “people.” Yet popular views have long shaped and challenged scientific concepts, methods, and notions of expertise. This course will explore the interactions between science, broadly conceived, and its diverse publics, with particular attention to moments of epistemic uncertainty and political controversy. How, we will ask, are scientific, technological, and medical publics made? How do they in turn shape the production of knowledge? We will consider how historians, science studies scholars, and cultural theorists have engaged such questions, in dialogue with scholarship about objectivity, biopolitics, and popular culture. Potential topics include visual cultures of science, medicine in the media, private enterprise and popular consumption, science in court, health activism, and more.

HMAN2402N.name: Economies of Truth: Rumors, Fake News, and Other Lies
HMAN2402N.description: While gossip and calumny have been circulating since time immemorial, they probably gained a renewed importance in the recent era of what is often described as “post-truth politics.” But what does “post-” exactly mean in “post-truth,” if lies and deceits have always been an integral part of the exercise of power? Our seminar will intertwine two threads: 1)  A genealogy of pseudology that includes Nietzsche’s “Truth and Lie in an Extra-Moral Sense,” Hannah Arendt’s “Truth and Politics,” Jacques Derrida’s “History of the Lie: Prolegomena,” Michel Foucault’s notion of parrēsia, and Gilles Deleuze’s readings of the “powers of the false.” 2) A series of guest lectures that will introduce current perspectives on rumors, fake news, nihilism, and conspiracy theories.

HMAN2402O.name: Nonhuman-Inhuman: Readings on the Boundaries of Humanity
HMAN2402O.description: With the aim of tracing and troubling the inner and outer contours of human agency, history, and meaning, this course puts writings on the nonhuman (nature-animal-technology) and the inhuman (culture-power-technique) in relation to each other to explore where and when boundaries of the human are exposed, strained, riddled, or put in crisis. Readings will prompt a reflection on histories of environment and inequity, “natural” disasters, situations of human-animal cohabitation or “conflict,” entanglements of human stories with those of extractions and flows of matter, and technology’s place in the production of contemporary (inter)species lives and deaths. Reading Mahasweta Devi, John Bellamy Foster, Judith Butler, Partha Chatterjee, Mariane Hirsch, Omer Bartov, Amitav Ghosh, Saidiya Hartman, Nasser Abourrahme, Richard Powers, and others, we will strive to cross and connect the disciplines of history, literature, environmental history, anthropology, and critical-cultural theory.

HMAN2410.name: Approaches to Environmental Humanities Research
HMAN2410.description: This collaborative, interdisciplinary seminar engages modes of inquiry in environmental humanities research and accounts for a range of theories and methods that encompass qualitative, historical, decolonial, and community-engaged scholarships, among others. The seminar focuses in particular on human and nonhuman relations and their impacts on environmental change, drawing on concepts and practices such as survivance, duration, weathering, extraction, and geological time. In addition to scholarly and theoretical texts, we will explore films, novels, creative nonfiction, and performances. Assignments help students engage and refine approaches to environmental scholarly inquiry and practice in a time of intensifying planetary and local crisis.

HMAN2971I.name: It’s About Time: Temporalities of Waiting, Suspension, and Rupture in Theory, Literature, and Film
HMAN2971I.description: This is a seminar on three forms of temporality — waiting, suspension, and rupture — and the coming to an end that all imply. These forms will be explored as pertaining to politics, theology, art, and experience. The work will be theoretical and hermeneutic; it will involve theoretical texts in political and critical theory and political theology, literary works, and films. We will explore time from the perspective of (its) ending. We will be interested in the prospect — whether a menace or a blessing — of a coming end, but also with the power and authority to bring an end, to an argument, to waiting in line, to a relationship, to life. We will study the power to suspend a coming end and the life under its shadow.

HNDI0100.name: Beginning Hindi or Urdu
HNDI0100.description: Introduces conversation, reading, and writing of modern standard Hindi and the Devanagari script. Those who already know Devanagari but have rusty conversation skills may join the class second semester; obtain instructor's permission during the first semester. Those who prefer to learn Urdu and the Persian script should contact the instructor.

HNDI0300.name: Intermediate Hindi-Urdu
HNDI0300.description: A continuation of HNDI 0100-0200, which is a prerequisite. Introduces the variation of the Arabic script used for Urdu. Prepares students to communicate in written and spoken language. Activities are conducted in Hindi/Urdu. Meets four hours weekly.

HNDI1080.name: Advanced Hindi-Urdu
HNDI1080.description: Each student follows an independent reading list determined in consultation with the instructor. The readings may include folk tales, journalistic prose, 20th-century literature, classical Urdu poetry of the 17th to 19th centuries, or subjects in nonfiction. The class meets together three hours weekly for discussion. Each student also spends one hour weekly with the instructor. Prerequisite: HNDI 0400.

HSP0310.name: Health Care in the United States
HSP0310.description: Introduction to the health care delivery system. An overview of the U.S. health care financing, delivery and regulatory system. Considers the interaction between paying for and providing and assuring the quality of health services; changes in one component of the system inevitably affect the others. Addresses the balance between employer funded health insurance, publicly funded health insurance and the consequences of not being insured. Six discussion sections will be arranged. Open to undergraduates only. This is a core class for the concentration in public health.

HSP1460.name: Public Health Law and Policy
HSP1460.description: Laws and policies shape public health in profound ways. The U.S. Constitution frames and limits government authority to protect and promote public health. It also provides protections for individual rights that often are in tension with public health’s focus on the common good. Federal, state and local laws and policies structure the distribution of society’s resources and—as interpreted, implemented and enforced—can have serious implications for health equity. The COVID-19 pandemic has exposed deeply polarized views among Americans about the role of government in public health and has laid bare vast structural health inequities. This course will explore the Constitutional foundations of public health law; how public health powers are distributed across different levels and branches of government; legal and policy strategies for addressing infectious and chronic diseases and injuries; and the role of laws and policies in structuring—and remedying—health inequities.

HSP1480.name: Foundations of Health Economics
HSP1480.description: This course builds an understanding of the healthcare delivery and financing systems from a health economics perspective. It will draw examples that illustrate the production of and demand for health, healthcare, and health insurance. The goals of the course are twofold. First, it will provide the basic intuition of the fundamental economic models such as health production, demand for healthcare and demand for insurance. Second, it will introduce key empirical findings in the public health economics literature. Emphasis will be placed on key theoretical insights as well as practical and public health policy implications.

HSP1481.name: Health Care Delivery Reform and Primary Care in the US
HSP1481.description: Health care delivery in the US is an enormous, complex, and fragmented system of hospitals, clinics, rehabilitation facilities and other services. These systems have matured under the payment incentives and culture of US health care to emphasize high volumes of services, often neglecting population health and patient experience as key goals. Increasing recognition that the current delivery system fails to deliver person-centered, high quality health care to populations has led to many delivery reform initiatives. These reforms are where the “rubber hits the road” for health systems shifting the status quo. The overall purpose of this course is to provide students with a strong foundation of knowledge on the current state of the US health care delivery system, the foundational role of primary care in its function and to develop tools to understand and critically evaluate major delivery reforms.

HSP1580.name: Pandemic Game Changers: Preparing the Next Generation of Decision-Makers for Emerging Bio Threats
HSP1580.description: Pandemic Game Changers will examine the public health and public policy issues vital to mitigating pandemic risks. It will afford students opportunities to analyze scenarios, identify and hone policy solutions, and learn how to convince decision-makers to take the steps needed to address the public health crises that pandemics cause. Students will be required to participate in interactive Q&A with field experts, perform a group analysis of an outbreak scenario, make a written and oral analysis of policy solutions for a biosecurity or biosafety risk, and provide a policy memo and persuasive oral briefing outlining views and potential next steps on one specific pandemic-related public policy issue.

HSP1821.name: Incarceration, Disparities, and Health
HSP1821.description: This survey course is designed for students who want to interrogate the central role that public health policies and practices play in creating and sustaining the nation’s epidemic of incarceration. The course will focus on individuals who have experienced incarceration and the under-resourced, low-income, and medically disenfranchised communities from which these individuals come and to which most will return. Students will learn about the lived experiences of those directly impacted by the criminal legal system through invited speakers who have been incarcerated. Experts who work at the intersection of the criminal legal and health systems will also be invited to the class.

HSP2081.name: Health Policy and Equity
HSP2081.description: While debates around health policy are often framed in empirical terms, ethical considerations are equally important, even if they often go unexamined. The objective of this course is to develop skills in the analysis of health policy and health systems through the application of both ethical reasoning and empirical frameworks, with an emphasis on questions of health equity throughout. This is accomplished through a broad engagement with prominent ethical frameworks, health care policy and system design, public health policy, and the social-structural determinants of health. The course relies heavily on case studies, which frame weekly classroom discussions that explore pressing debates in health policy.

HSP2410E.name: Medicare: A Data Based Policy Examination
HSP2410E.description: This course will explore the role of Medicare as America's health insurer for the elderly and disabled through the use of real Medicare insurance claims data, examining how Medicare policy changes in financing and regulation have affected the delivery and receipt of medical services. At the end of the course students will: 1) know the history of important Medicare policy changes; 2) be able to construct aggregated patient case mix acuity adjusted measures of provider quality using insurance claims data; 3) be able to conduct policy analyses using Medicare claims data that are sensitive to standardized coding schemes. Enrollment limited to 15 graduate students. Prerequisite: PHP 2120, 2508, or 2510. Instructor permission required.

HSP2412.name: Embedding Research in Practice: A Learning Health Systems Approach
HSP2412.description:
This course offers students an immersive experience in learning health systems (LHS) and community-based participatory research, focusing on pragmatic research supporting real-world decision-making and quality improvement. The course prepares students with foundational knowledge and experience in designing and conducting LHS projects. The course combines classroom-based seminar discussions and presentations with partnered research opportunities to provide students with a foundation in the intersecting fields of LHS research, partner engagement, quality improvement and implementation science, equipping them to contribute meaningfully to projects that generate timely, relevant, and useful information to help healthcare partners improve.
Classroom-based lectures and discussions will characterize key components of the LHS, the cycle of learning, and highlight a range of LHS research competencies.  Through partnerships with healthcare organizations, students will gain hands-on experience engaging providers as collaborators, building partnerships, and applying research methods to real-world needs and contexts.

HSP2445.name: Minding the Gap: The U.S. Healthcare Safety Net
HSP2445.description: The right to access affordable, quality health care in the US is not guaranteed.  During our nation’s history, a patchwork quilt of programs, referred to collectively as the safety net, has been crafted to address health care needs for a wide range of people who fall through the cracks.  This course examines its structure, function, and effects. We introduce key features of the safety net: access, cost, quality, and outcomes. We pay particular attention to the nation’s largest program, Medicaid.  We highlight the unique challenges facing vulnerable groups: legal and illegal immigrants, homeless populations, veterans, and people with disabilities.

HSP2446.name: Health Care Financing and Delivery
HSP2446.description:
The purpose of the course is to foster your development into a health services and policy researcher.  To accomplish this, the course involves a general survey of substantive issues in payment and financing in healthcare.
By the end of the course you should have knowledge of the main institutions, policy issues, and research areas and questions related to payment and financing in US healthcare.  You should also have an initial understanding of where the most promising and pressing areas of research lie within this field.  Thus, this course is about the past, present, and future of the field.

HSP2455A.name: Health Services Research Methods I
HSP2455A.description: Health services researchers use theories, models, and data to understand the health care system, assess the effectiveness of interventions (at multiple levels of the healthcare system), and inform health policy decisions. This course reviews the application of statistical and epidemiological principles to the design and analysis of health services research studies. The goal is to familiarize students with common study designs and methods in health services research, so that they can critically review the published literature and use these approaches in their own research.

HSP2465A.name: Introduction to Health Decision Analysis
HSP2465A.description: Many decisions in health are value-laden, involve competing objectives, or must be made under uncertainty. Health decision analysis is a structured approach to thinking through such decisional problems. This course introduces decision analysis and cost-effectiveness analysis for public health and clinical problems. It covers basic theory for decisionmaking; principles and techniques for mathematical modeling; and implementation, by analyzing archetypical decisional problems in health. Pre Requisites: Some facility with mathematical notation and basic concepts in probability (advanced undergraduate students can enroll after instructor approval). Recommended course: DATA 1010, MATH 1610, or APMA 1690.

IAPA0400.name: Fiscal Plumbing 101: The American Tax State in Comparative and Historical  Perspective
IAPA0400.description: This IAPA Gateway course explores the origins and development of the American Tax State in comparative and historical perspective. It's designed as an interdisciplinary introduction to the welter of problems associated with the raising and spending of public revenue –the life blood of contemporary nation-states. It should be of use to students interested in the political and institutional development of the welfare state, and in the origins, fault lines and prospects of American federalism. We explore the origins and development of the American Tax State in comparative and historical perspective. It is designed as an interdisciplinary introduction to the welter of problems associated with the raising and spending of public revenue –the life blood of contemporary nation-states.

IAPA1002.name: Foundations of Policy and Governance
IAPA1002.description: An overview of policymaking and policy analysis in the contemporary United States. The course begins with an examination of traditional justifications for government action. We will then examine the discipline of policy analysis that has arisen to design and evaluate public policies. We will also consider critiques of the rational method and ask questions about how policy expertise fits into the political system. The course ends with classic works on organizations and implementation. Not open to graduate students.

IAPA1003.name: Foundations of Security
IAPA1003.description: This course introduces students to contemporary international security topics with a special focus on problems associated with war and violent conflict in the 21st century. It mixes the theoretical, historical, analytical, and practical. Students learn theory on the causes of war, how wars are fought, civil-military relations, the costs and consequences of warfare, and more. They also learn about the organization of the U.S. and other national security establishments. Using these tools, we will apply social science methods and critical thinking to security “hot spots” and wars around the world. There will be an emphasis on analyzing the unfolding war in Ukraine, as well as the prospects for U.S.-China rivalry and/or military conflict in the future, including within a Taiwan scenario. Aside from readings, lectures and discussions, students will benefit from a variety of films, simulations, walking excursions, and debates.

IAPA1020A.name: Politics of the Illicit Global Economy (POLS 1020)
IAPA1020A.description: Interested students must register for POLS 1020.

IAPA1201C.name: Introduction to International Macroeconomics
IAPA1201C.description: This goal of this class is to introduce students to current issues in international macro. The class will cover 6 broad issues. For each issue we’ll start with an introduction and examples, discuss some of the state-of-the-art knowledge around it, and then cover the following: -Empirical work: establishing the relevant facts, where to get the data from, how to process the data -Minimal theoretical framework: using data and theory to better understand the issue -Policy/business impact: how is the issue relevant for business participants and/or policy makers Class is designed for students interested in a career in international organizations, for students interested in an introduction to academic research in international macro, and finally for business-oriented students who want to get a better grasp of the international macroeconomic landscape.

IAPA1201D.name: Social Entrepreneurship
IAPA1201D.description: Social Entrepreneurship, engages students in the process of exploring significant global problems and developing innovative solutions that drive transformative social change. The course helps students understand the strategies that social entrepreneurs employ to tackle complex and entrenched social problems with transformative approaches that work and impact systems. Students will learn about real organizations and interact with entrepreneurs leading this work.  Case studies, complemented by articles and guest speakers, will show different approaches to social entrepreneurship and illustrate the strengths and weaknesses of various models and strategies.

IAPA1201G.name: Tech, Money and Violence: How Innovation Shapes Our World
IAPA1201G.description: Technology is the glue that puts together social order – or creates disorder. In this class we will discuss three types of technologies that have radically transformed in recent years: information technologies (social media), financial technologies (money) and weapons. Information technologies can we weaponized (surveillance, manipulation, disinformation), information technologies change the way we transact (Venmo, crypto), the scarier weapons are no longer nuclear but affordable drones. All these developments are connected and mutually-constitutive in ways that we still need to understand: How did they come about? Why did they come about? And how do they change our lives?

IAPA1201H.name: Diplomacy, Crisis, and War in the Modern Era
IAPA1201H.description: This undergraduate course examines war and peace after 1945 through the lens of international relations (IR) theory. It aims to both teach students theoretical perspectives on international relations and to critically evaluate the changing ways in which states have interacted with one another since the end of World War II. What caused the Cold War? Did nuclear weapons change the way that states negotiated with one another? How much did individuals make a difference during interstate crises? Why did states sometimes fail to reach peaceful settlements with one another? What were the experiences of states other than the United States and Soviet Union during the Cold War? How have social and economic institutions changed international politics in the twenty-first century?

IAPA1225.name: Nuclear Weapons (POLS 1225)
IAPA1225.description: Interested students must register for POLS 1225.
